#9177. Forma Is a Wearable Viewfinder Built for Finding Photo Compositions

Forma Is a Wearable Viewfinder Built for Finding Photo Compositions

Canadian photographer and inventor Peter Modzelewski has launched Forma on Kickstarter via his independent photo gear studio, Oramod. It is a pocket-sized optical viewfinder designed for a wide range of film and digital cameras.

Forma utilizes interchangeable, laser-cut cards tailored to specific formats and focal lengths, ranging from 35mm film cameras to large-format and specialized panoramic systems.

Photographers can simply hold Forma up to their eye to accurately preview a composition without setting up their camera—a process that can be quite an ordeal with certain medium- and large-format systems. It can also be used when scouting locations to help photographers determine where to position their gear in advance.

Forma can also be used on cameras without viewfinders, spanning specialized analog cameras to modern digital compacts like the Ricoh GR series.

As Modzelewski explains, Forma is constructed from a 3D-printed, carbon-fiber-infused composite material, offering a rugged yet lightweight design weighing just 30 grams (just over an ounce). It is built on the binocular fusion principle used in Voigtländer’s Kontur viewfinder from 1951. However, unlike the Kontur, Forma is highly configurable thanks to its interchangeable framing cards.

Forma features built-in illumination for low-light conditions, gels that color-tint the framelines for visibility in various environments, and a quick-release mounting system that allows photographers to switch between wearing it around the neck and attaching it to a camera in seconds.

“Worn around the neck, Forma helps photographers train their eye to recognize what their lenses will see, explore compositions before setting up a camera, and compare focal lengths by easily swapping cards,” Modzelewski says.

“Mounted on-camera, Forma provides a framing reference while allowing photographers to anticipate moments unfolding beyond the boundaries of a conventional viewfinder.”

Modzelewski sent pre-production units to photographers worldwide for real-world testing, including Japanese photographer Kazutoshi Yoshimura and British landscape photographer Lee Pengelly.

“I was amazed at how clearly I could see the field of view corresponding to the focal length of my lens,” Yoshimura says.

“It will be an essential part of my kit from now on,” adds Pengelly.

Utah-based large-format photographer James Holland touted Forma’s accuracy, noting that he didn’t have to move his tripod “an inch” when framing with it.

Forma is available to back on Kickstarter now, starting at $55 CAD (approximately $39 USD) for early birds. The campaign reached its funding goal quickly on launch day and has nearly 60 backers at the time of writing. Forma is expected to begin shipping to backers next month.

#9176. Nat Meade's "Franklin" @ HESSE FLATOW, NYC

HESSE FLATOW is pleased to announce the opening of Franklin, an exhibition of paintings and works on paper by Nat Meade, marking his third solo presentation with the gallery. The show is on view through April 18, 2026.

The emotional arc of life’s struggles and triumphs take shape within Meade’s figurative works, reflecting the artist’s everyday experiences as he navigates being a father, son, partner, and academic. Far from portraits of actual individuals, his protagonists mirror timeless archetypes. At times, we encounter a lone traveler searching for existential validation; at other times, we see through intergenerational dynamics. This allegorical distance via painting provides a realm for Meade to explore personal challenges through absurd, somber, and humorous tropes, while also furnishing a space rife with human nature that bears unequivocal resonance.

Meade’s reflections on his relationship with his father after his recent passing, and subsequent reevaluations of his own role as a parent percolate throughout the works in the exhibition. Vulnerability, pain, and mortality are themes Meade does not shy away from, yet the introduction of younger males in this body of work casts a sense of hope, acceptance, reconciliation, and renewal.

Faced with a pair of dangling legs from a cloud in Poise, we question whether a figure is ascending or descending from the heavens, a suggestion perhaps on the interchangeability of birth and death, be it physical or spiritual. Ghostly specters hover over certain individuals – a metaphor for inherited trauma and release. In the same way that a soul peels away from an expiring body in classic cartoons, we observe a spirit looking back on itself with what might be  happiness or regret. The exhibition’s title Franklin is a subtle nod to the 1974 horror film Texas Chainsaw Massacre, known for its portrayal of a deranged patriarchal family. Meade embraces this inner turmoil of contending with one’s violent and antagonistic impulses as his characters are visibly sublimated or put in their place. A vulture picking away at a corpse recalls the eternal punishment of Prometheus by Zeus, while a bearded figure on his hands and knees echoes William Blake’s portrayal of Nebuchadnezzar, condemned for his lust for power.

In contrast to the adults, Meade’s younger figures appear more harmonious. A young boy charts his own path as he steers a boat with a radiant torch, unclouded by societal and familial pressures. A sense of childlike wonder and adventure beholds an adolescent ankle-deep in a secluded cove, reaching in to touch the sea floor brilliantly covered in starfish, anemones, and mussels. In a related work, we observe two pairs of legs belonging to father and son in the same shallow pool, one tenderly guiding the other. Having in the past shown his figures wrestling with or victims of forces of nature, physically being overtaken by turbulent wind and crashing waves, Meade’s focus on calmer seas signals a turning point. He recognizes the need to acknowledge one’s rocky histories in order to heal and release future generations from similar burdens. Despite what may seem like an insurmountable heaviness, he reminds us of the stubborn resilience of human nature, making progress attainable.

#9174. Inside OM Digital Solutions’ Okaya Manufacturing Site

Inside OM Digital Solutions’ Okaya Manufacturing Site

I know how to take pictures, but ask me how the lens on my camera is made and I have a lot less to say. A visit to the Okaya Manufacturing Site in Japan, followed by some research afterward, gave me a lesson in a subject I’d never understood particularly well. I wanted to understand how the glass inside a lens is crafted, how the tools used in that process are prepared, and how people learn to do that work.

The facility was OM Digital Solutions’ Okaya Manufacturing Site in Nagano Prefecture, Japan. This was an overwhelming experience from a learning standpoint, so there was quite a bit that went over my head as we moved from station to station. Luckily, follow-up discussions with OM SYSTEM and research helped me fill in some of the gaps.

Okaya is the first optical lens manufacturing site in Japan for OM Digital Solutions, the company behind OM SYSTEM. It opened in 2025 and does two jobs. It produces lenses that are made in small quantities but come in many different types, and it works as a pilot factory, a place where the manufacturing processes for technically demanding new lenses are developed and proven before they’re used at scale.

The site works closely with the optical design team at the company’s headquarters in Hachioji, Tokyo. Designing a lens and figuring out how to build it are two different jobs that call for different expertise. Okaya’s engineers handle the second one, turning a design into a production process that actually works.

Mass production happens at the company’s factory in Vietnam. Before a production line for a new lens launches there, Okaya verifies the production technology, the manufacturing processes, and the work methods it will use. Working those out in Japan first is meant to make production in Vietnam more efficient and keep the quality consistent.

The place to begin is with an individual lens element, one of the many pieces of glass inside a camera lens. OM SYSTEM’s M.Zuiko Digital ED 40-150mm F2.8 PRO, for example, contains 16 of these elements. Before the lens can be assembled, each of these pieces of glass needs the correct curve and a smooth surface.

A piece of glass can be clear and look correct but still bend light the wrong way. A lens bends light to bring an image into focus on the camera’s sensor. Light from each point in the scene needs to come together at a matching point on the sensor. The curves of the glass help direct it there. If a curve is wrong, that light can spread around its intended point instead, making a small detail look blurry.

The sequence OM SYSTEM showed us at the Okaya Manufacturing Site starts with grinding, which gradually wears down the glass to form the basic curve. Finer grinding makes smaller adjustments to the glass. Polishing then wears away more material to give the surface the smoothness and accuracy it needs.

I got a small taste of this myself. During a workshop at Okaya, I tried lens polishing, including mounting the lens and taking it off again afterward. It looked simple. Then a slight mistake in my setup chipped the lens. That was enough to show me how delicate the process is and how much care and precision it takes.

Glass can look clear and smooth to the naked eye and still have flaws that affect the photograph. Tiny scratches, bumps, and dips, or a surface that strays slightly from its intended shape, can scatter light in directions it shouldn’t go. That can cause flare, the haze or bright spots stray light leaves in a picture, and lower the contrast, so the image looks flatter.

If the surface doesn’t match its designed shape, light won’t bend and come together the way the designers intended. So polishing has two jobs: leave the surface free of scratches, and reproduce the designed shape to within nanometers, or billionths of a meter. The engineers check the glass with a range of measuring instruments, but they also rely on experience and skill to make delicate adjustments to each lens.

Then they have to do it again on the next piece of glass, and the one after that. Even a slight difference between individual lenses can change how light travels through the finished lens and affect image quality.

Each glass element also needs to sit in the right position inside the lens. Imagine fitting one into a holder. It could fit neatly while the curved faces that bend light sit slightly off-center. That mismatch can send light to the wrong place. A manufacturing step called centering corrects that mismatch before assembly.

Getting the curve right and getting the glass into the right position both matter to the photograph. Even when we focus correctly, errors in the glass’s shape or alignment can leave fine details looking soft.

Even the tools OM Digital Solutions uses at the Okaya Manufacturing Site need preparation before they can work on the glass. These are the parts fitted to the machines that grind and polish the lens elements. The tools the engineers use to work on the glass need smooth, accurately made surfaces, too.

One of these tools has a small, round face that touches the glass. To prepare it, an engineer uses a second tool: a disc on the end of a handle. The engineer holds the disc against the first tool’s face, polishing the two surfaces together.

The accuracy of the tool affects the accuracy of the surface it produces on the glass.

I was surprised to see that they still prepare some of their tools by hand. The precision required helped me appreciate the care the engineers bring to preparing those tools and building the lenses. At Okaya, I saw veteran engineers working alongside younger colleagues to pass on their skills. Both generations were full of excitement and pride as they showed us how they make lenses in their facility.

That exchange between generations is a big part of how the skills developed at the Okaya Manufacturing Site get passed down. OM Digital Solutions says the younger engineers’ questions also encourage the veterans to keep improving their own skills. While watching them work, I could see how explaining a familiar task to someone else can make you think more carefully about the way you do it.

The training follows an apprenticeship model, with coaching taking place during manufacturing work such as polishing. Part of the challenge is passing on knowledge that comes from experience and can be difficult to put into written instructions.

With its younger engineers in mind, the company is also exploring other ways to pass on the skills and judgment that are hard to capture in a written document.

Along with their manufacturing skills, OM Digital Solutions also wants the experienced engineers to pass on their way of thinking about the work.

If I were explaining one of my photographs to another photographer, I’d want to talk about why I chose a particular aperture for depth of field or focused on a certain part of the scene. Understanding those choices could help them make decisions about their own photographs. Knowing why a manufacturing step is done a certain way could help younger engineers decide what to keep and where to make improvements. They can build on that experience to improve both how lenses are made and how those lenses perform.

When a photographer buys a lens, they expect it to meet the same standard as other copies of that model. That depends on being able to make its components accurately, again and again.

At Okaya, engineers test early versions of lens components for new products. They also check new manufacturing methods to see whether they are suitable for producing lenses in larger quantities. Once those methods have been checked, they can be transferred to the factory in Vietnam.

Some of this involves tasks as routine as loading parts into machines and taking them out again. They are automating repetitive jobs like these to help improve production quality and efficiency.

The relationship between the two sites continues long after production begins. If an issue turns up while a mass-production process is being verified at the Vietnam factory, the team at Okaya can reproduce the same issue on purpose. Recreating it gives the engineers a controlled way to analyze what went wrong, find the root cause, and develop a fix. Each round of that back-and-forth turns highly specialized know-how into a process the factory can repeat with the same quality, lens after lens.

Learning about OM Digital Solutions’ Okaya Manufacturing Site helped me understand the work, passion, and dedication that go into their lens making. I had never given the process much thought and, I admit, I assumed it was easier than it actually is. The hand preparation of the tools was a good example. Once I understood how a tool’s accuracy affects the glass it works on, I could see why that preparation needed so much care.

It also showed me how seriously the company takes quality. Nearly every step I learned about, from measuring a polished surface to deliberately recreating a problem from the Vietnam factory, exists to make sure a lens performs the way it was designed to, and that the next copy does too.

Understanding the work gave me more respect for the engineers who showed it to us and for the experience they are passing on to younger colleagues. As a travel photographer, I’ve often taken my gear for granted. I now have a better idea of what goes into making a lens and a much greater appreciation for the lenses that have helped me document the world over the last 15 years.

#9173. Chris “Daze” Ellis "Orchid Rain on the Underground" @ PPOW Gallery, NYC

PPOW are pleased to present Orchid Rain on the Underground, Chris “Daze” Ellis’s third solo exhibition with the gallery. The show is on view through April 25, 2026. Featuring a new series of paintings, multimedia installation, and a site-specific mural, the exhibition harnesses the passion and spontaneity of the graffiti movement of the 1970s and 80s while demonstrating a thoughtful and meticulous practice honed over the past five decades. While the version of New York City that fostered Daze’s beginnings as a fine artist may feel like a bygone era, the works in this exhibition are evidence of its enduring legacy. By revitalizing that foundational energy for the present moment, Daze affirms the continued relevance of those figures and places, and their profound influence on the creative spirit that persists throughout the city today.

Born in Brooklyn in 1962, Daze became inspired by early graffiti writers like Blade, Lee Quiñones, and PHASE 2 while attending High School of Art and Design in the mid 1970s. As he began to establish his own name as an artist, he was also a frequent visitor to what would become historic landmarks of the city’s nightlife, including the Lit Lounge in the East Village, Danceteria on West 21st Street, and the Mudd Club in Tribeca. These nightclubs, which often doubled as art galleries and performance venues, functioned as generative sites of social and artistic experimentation and part of the driving force behind Daze’s early works. By the early 1980s, he had begun transitioning from tagging subway cars to developing a studio practice that encapsulates the ethos of the city.

Inspired by early 20th-century urban realist artists, including John Sloan of the Ashcan School and Reginald Marsh of the WPA era, Daze’s works honor New York City’s streets and subways as important sites of his creative evolution. Simultaneously influenced by the lyrical abstraction of works by Joan Mitchell and Willem De Kooning, Daze combines gestural swaths of acrylic and spray paint with detailed renderings of train car interiors, tunnels, and stations. In Gem Spa In the 80s, 2025, Daze depicts the now iconic newspaper stand and candy store that once operated on the corner of St. Mark’s Place and Second Avenue. Gem Spa was a central destination and meeting place for members of the city’s subcultures and is referenced by literary figures like Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg (who called it a “nerve center” of the city). Important people from Daze’s life can be found throughout the composition, among them critic and curator Carlo McCormick as well as artist Martin Wong, who both emerge amongst the crowd in the painting’s foreground. In other works, technicolor throngs of flowers ascend from heaps of urban rubble, representing optimism amidst inequality and the beauty that can arise out of destruction. Throughout the exhibition, these varied combinations of tropical flora and local flowers from the artist’s home in upstate New York function as poignant memorials to what has been lost and hopeful testaments to the beauty and creativity that can still be found around every corner.

The exhibition will also include a site-specific mural, bringing an aspect of Daze’s practice often relegated to the outdoors into the interior setting of the gallery. Covering the walls of a hallway, the mural gives way to the final room of the gallery, featuring a multimedia installation that transports viewers into a composite scene from the artist’s youth. Combining a light-up dance floor and disco ball, actual subway car seats, and a curated track fusing house, disco, hip-hop, and club music, the installation emphasizes the freedom and creative inspiration that arose from these settings, and their importance to Daze’s personal and artistic development. Combining elements from throughout his career, Orchid Rain on the Underground showcases Daze’s never-ending exploration of daily life in New York City while paying homage to the people and places that comprise its vibrant cultural heartbeat.

#9172. Peruvian senator calls for removal of large-scale replicas of Moche erotic sculptures from public park

One of the huaco erótico sculptures in Fertility Park, near Trujillo, Peru Photo: Richard Avila, via Wikimedia Commons

A controversy over 3m-tall erotic sculptures in northern Peru reignited recently after a senator requested that the cultural ministry remove them from a public area. Located in a park outside the city of Trujillo, the sculptures are replicas of ceramics from the pre-Incan Moche civilisation.

“What happens when children see these images? Neurological and psychological factors are affected, because they see body dimensions that are completely different from how they see themselves,” Milagros Jáuregui, a conservative senator from the Renovación Popular party, said in a speech on 26 October.

The sculptures are located in Parque de la Fertilidad (Fertility Park), a public space where in 2021 then-mayor Arturo Fernández of the Moche district began installing giant fibreglass reproductions of ceramic depictions of sexual acts to promote tourism.

Known as huacos eróticos, the much smaller original ceramics date from the 3rd to 8th century AD. No more than 30cm in height, they were placed in tombs as burial offerings. But the debate about their much larger versions in the park goes beyond political prudishness.

“It’s a complicated issue,” the Peruvian archaeologist Walter Alva tells The Art Newspaper. “There’s freedom to express or re-create themes from the past, but these ceramics were created to be placed as offerings to the dead, with a sense of revitalising life. They are associated with both fertility and an entire system of beliefs.”

An original huaco erótico ceramic offering made by the Moche civilisation, Larco Museum, Lima Photo: László Varga, via Wikimedia Commons

The Moche civilisation covered 700km of the coast of what is now Peru, between the regions of Piura and Ancash, centuries before the Inca dominated the area. “Moche art is primarily ceramic, and these vessels depict erotic scenes or concepts of sexuality from that era,” Alva says. “The sculptures in the park were created outside of their historical context.”

One of the greatest archaeological discoveries from the Moche civilisation was that of the Lord of Sipán near the city of Chiclayo—a discovery Alva made in 1987. A 3rd-century monarch, the Lord of Sipán’s body was found covered with gold along with eight other people, a dog and two llamas and nearly 500 objects including ceramic vessels, ornaments and textiles.

The Moche have the largest number of erotic representations among pre-Hispanic civilisations. The most complete collection of its ceramics is in Lima, at the Larco Museum of pre-Columbian art, which celebrated its centennial in July. Before the 1960s, children were forbidden from entering the room that housed the huacos. Today, minors must be accompanied by an adult. The institution’s Erotic Gallery is one of its most popular attractions.

Jáuregui, an evangelical pastor as well as a senator, believes these Moche sculptures should only be in closed spaces. “Displaying these types of images in public is harmful to children,” she told congress. “We should have them in museums, where high-school students can observe a part of our culture that is a national treasure with the help of teachers or some kind of tutor.”

The well-preserved statue is one of the oldest artefacts discovered in the Chan Chan archaeological site

Excavations at the Cerro Mayal site in the north of the country show it was an important production facility for Moche ceramics around the seventh century

#9170. William N. Copley "X-Rated (1972–1974)" @ Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin

Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin, is pleased to announce X-Rated (1972–1974), a solo exhibition of paintings and works on paper by William N. Copley. This is the fourth presentation of the artist’s work at the gallery, and the show will be on view through April 22, 2026.

Copley came to painting from an unusual position. He had ambitions to become a writer before becoming a painter, and, for a brief period in the late 1940s, he co-founded and operated a gallery in Beverly Hills that focused on the Surrealists. The Copley Galleries – which he ran with his brother-in-law, the artist John Ployardt – brought him into close contact with exiled Surrealists such as Man Ray, Max Ernst and Marcel Duchamp, as well as the dealer Alexander Iolas, who encouraged him to pursue his nascent art practice. Adopting the signature CPLY around the time the gallery closed, he debuted his first exhibition at a bookstore in Los Angeles in 1951, shortly before he moved to France.Even though he was a generation younger than the Surrealists, Copley’s work is deeply informed by the movement on a conceptual and personal level. While his bold black outlines and self-taught figurative style recall comics and Pop art, Copley approached painting with a literary sensibility, using narrative strategies that both embodied Surrealist principles and drove the structural evolution of his compositions. Like many Surrealists, Copley embraced humour, psychology and eroticism as fundamental to his creative process, yet his engagement with overtly sexual subjects went far beyond the playful eroticism of his peers.On view in the exhibition are works from Copley’s prolific ‘X-Rated’ series, created between 1972 and 1975, and first exhibited in 1974 in an eponymous show at the New York Cultural Center. This body of work draws on erotic imagery and ritualised motifs from adult magazines, seeking, in the artist’s own words, to ‘break through the barrier of pornography into the area of joy.’ 1In a decade when the sale of hardcore pornography was still illegal in the United States, Copley would buy ‘adult magazines’ under the counter, using them as a source for inventive figurative and narrative paintings that explored eroticism, sexual politics and the pursuit of pleasure. The artist was able to convey a wide range of tone in the ‘X-Rated’ paintings: some, such as The Seven Year Itch, 1973, are tender; others, including  Viridiana, 1973, are exuberant; and almost all of them are openly humorous. Underscoring the open-endedness of sexual expression, Copley stated: ‘That’s what makes sex so much fun: since nobody really understands it, the possibilities for originality are endless.’ 2Copley typically produced two stages of preparatory drawings before starting a painting: an initial, small-scale study, followed by a larger version in which he refined the composition, introduced changes, and heightened the work’s pictorial dynamism. The resulting paintings maintain a deliberately slapdash style, with figures treated loosely rather than meticulously rendered. The exhibition makes this developmental process visible through multiple pairings of preparatory drawings and completed paintings, including Calcutta, 1973, and its counterpart Untitled, 1973.Scenes of copulations and orgies are set against vivid, brightly coloured backgrounds animated by bold, geometric patterns, making them almost ‘too artful to be libidinous, let alone lascivious’, as critic James R. Mellow has remarked. 3 It is both this treatment of the backgrounds and the contorted, entwined bodies with their attenuated limbs and schematic outlines that has prompted critics to draw a link between Copley and Henri Matisse more than once. Yet, while depictions of the nude and sexual imagery throughout art history have traditionally relied on suggestion and idealisation, Copley presents the sexual act directly, leaving nothing to the imagination.With titles borrowed from Hollywood movies such as Les Quatre Cent Coups, The Exorcist or Tobacco Road, Copley tempered the shock of the pornographic image through comic playfulness and pop cultural sensibility. Manifesting a Surrealist disjunction, the movies rarely align explicitly with the images’ content, but the titles nevertheless set in motion a cascade of associations for the viewer. The title of the series, likewise, draws on terminology from the film industry: until the 1990s, the film-classification term ‘X-rated’ was used in the US for films only suitable for adults. Despite the cautionary notices that some visitors might find the subject matter offensive, the 1974 exhibition at the Cultural Center – curated by the newly appointed and strikingly progressive director Mario Amaya – received a notably positive critical response. Art in America writer Peter Schjeldahl hailed the presentation as a ‘uniformly gorgeous exhibition,’ noting that it marked ‘a highly satisfying development in Copley’s work’. 4The ‘X-Rated’ series represents a singular chapter in Copley’s oeuvre, deliberately set apart from the prevailing currents of the early-1970s art scene. Even in today’s uncensored and image-saturated world, Copley’s suggestive canvases retain a subversive charge. By merging art and eroticism, Copley challenged conservative norms and rejected the notion of artistic neutrality, clearing away moralistic constraints in favour of directness and humour.

#9169. Is Sexy Art Back, or Is It Just Me?

From Willem de Kooning’s miserable nudes to Alexandra Barth’s hot and bothered architecture, sex is in the air in Chicago.

CHICAGO — I see a lot of exhibitions in Chicago, and lately, I have been noticing more than a few that feel almost ridiculously erotic. I mean, I get it, there's always been plenty of eros in art, but I haven't observed it much lately at the school where I teach nor in the shows that I view. Is sex back? Or it could just be me. I turned 50 this past year, and popular culture suggests that this might be what happens around my age, à la Sharon Horgan's Youth and Olivia Colman's Wicker, both recent screen-based explorations of lusty midlife ladyhood.

For those who have never had one or maybe never will, female middle-age libido sets at either zero or 1,000, on a scale of one to 100. It is not an easy ride. Shifting from one state to the other causes severe whiplash for driver and passengers alike. That’s based on an admittedly minuscule survey, though fear not, this will not be a personal essay about my own sexuality or that of my acquaintances. God, no. Maybe after everyone’s dead. What proceeds, instead, is a round-up of exhibitions that, for me, have a strong connecting thread, obviously red, and not discussed much if at all in the various associated didactics.

What shows? Last spring, Alice Tippit’s sly, meticulous paintings at the DePaul Art Museum had me thinking I probably needed to start talking to a therapist again, because what was going on in my head was not articulated anywhere in the otherwise delightful catalogue. Not even close. During the summer, SHADOW at tête-à-tête-à-tête, a wicked little curatorial project of Shannon Stratton, included Holly Murkerson’s sensuous photographs of a stone passageway worth entering and two dark leather-and-wood stools by David Sprecher and Neiva Mulhearn that required straddling and peering into.

What wasn’t a turn-on was the Art Institute of Chicago’s summer blockbuster, Willem de Kooning Drawing. You wouldn’t know from the glowing reviews or polite museum text that miserable naked women filled the walls. I like a good nude as much as anyone, but at some point, maybe it was the third room — definitely by the time I got to the giant rowboat charcoals of the mid-60s — de Kooning’s subjects started to look like crime victims.

Left: Lee Miller, “Woman with Hand on Head” (also known as “Coiffure”) (1931), photograph; right: Lee Miller, “Charlie Chaplin with chandelier" (1932), photograph (both photos courtesy Art Institute of Chicago)

#9168. Collector Elie Khouri to create physical home for his private foundation in Dubai

A rendering of the Elie Khouri Art Foundation in Dubai

The Dubai-based art collector Elie Khouri is building a space in the city for his eponymous foundation. The Elie Khouri Art Foundation (Ekaf) will be located in the coastal district of Jumeirah 1, in a villa renovated and redesigned by Counterspace, a firm led by the architect Sumayya Vally. The space, expected to open in 2028, will host public exhibitions and educational programmes.

Khouri is one of the Unite Arab Emirates (UAE)’s biggest and best-known collectors. Originally from Lebanon, he made his name as the chief executive officer of Omnicom Media in the Middle East and North Africa, and has been based in Dubai since the 1990s.

He began making plans for the foundation around five years ago, as one of the London-based Deflina Foundation’s collectors-in-residence, a programme launched in 2017 that considers collecting as a practice and seeks to support more ambitious implementation. With them he conducted feasibility studies to better understand what Dubai needs.

“The whole idea is to give back and foster exchange of ideas, challenge thinking and bring new perspectives,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “Dubai is about entrepreneurship. They support people like me, people coming to fulfil their ambitions. And what Dubai needs is private institutions, because that's how they will build their own version of culture.”

Despite Dubai’s large number of artists and galleries, it has never had a major museum, and private foundations have become a significant part of its infrastructure. The Jameel Arts Centre and Alserkal Avenue, each backed by individuals, are the two pillars of the art scene, in addition to smaller foundations such as Ishara, which focuses on art from South Asia.

Ekaf has an emphasis on global contemporary art, though one in which art from the Middle East will play an important role.

“We are here to support talent internationally,” says Khouri. “We're not about the region, but since we are in the Middle East, we also look at the best talent here. We have a responsibility to the ecosystem and the galleries.”

Ekaf will take Khouri’s collection, comprising works by more than 300 artists, as its starting point, drawing from it for initial exhibitions. Later shows will increasingly involve loans and collaborations. Ultimately, Khouri intends to establish an Ekaf collection that is separate to his personal holdings.

The veteran art strategist Caroline Louca, who was formerly at Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism and Christie’s Middle East, has been appointed as the director of the foundation. Louca and Khouri are looking to hire a curatorial team closer to the completion date for the museum.

Louca underlines that community engagement will be a major part of the foundation, with plans for talks, lectures and education streams. The foundation’s location, in Jumeirah 1, is a bonus in this respect. Jumeirah 1 is one of the oldest neighbourhoods in Dubai, where many affluent long-time residents live. Ekaf’s villa was home to an Emirati family in the 1980s, and Vally’s designs retain the elements of old-school Gulf architecture that is a source of nostalgia for many in the UAE.

"We are focusing on how we can make a place become part of the community—and not just focus on what we’re showing,” says Louca. “You can see beautiful artworks everywhere, but we want people to be a bit daring. We want them to walk in and ask questions—and not be embarrassed to ask questions—and then come back and ask more. If we can achieve that, it will be our barometer of success.”

The private institution, funded by Al Futtaim Group, will be built on a jetty

#9167. An Interview with Surreal Salon 18 Winner, River Reishi

We are so excited to share our interview with Surreal Salon 18 winner, River Reishi, selected by guest juror, Swoon. On the occasion of the win, we spoke with Reishi about the work in the show, the history of Surreal Salon, and her upcoming travels.

Juxtapoz: Congrats on the big win! Talk about the winning work, what the story behind it is, the process, and even the process of submitting it to the Surreal Salon?River Reishi: The piece is called Surface Tension. It shows a figure emerging from dark water, her hands reaching forward as if she is about to break through the surface and step into our world. She is half submerged, suspended in that strange moment between two realms. Around her is an ephemeral field of black sand and amber.

From land, the surface of water looks smooth and transparent, almost empty. But of course it hides an entire world that is not ours. I have always been fascinated by that threshold. The installation tries to hold that exact moment where the two worlds meet.

The sculpture also glows faintly from within, which was a little hard to see in the bright gallery lighting but becomes visible as you approach. I like that quiet surprise. The piece looks still at first, but there is a sense that something is about to happen. Water is often a symbol of life, but it also carries danger and power. Louisiana and the Gulf region know that reality very well. I think some of that tension found its way into the work.

The black sand surrounding the sculpture is loose and hand-drawn into patterns, so the installation only exists in that form for a short time. Even small vibrations change it. I am interested in that fragility, in works that cannot quite stay fixed.

It was already an honor to be included in a show curated by Caledonia Curry (Swoon). When I arrived to install the piece and saw the other works for the first time, I remember thinking how haunting and memorable every single one was. So hearing the piece announced as Best in Show later that night felt surreal in the truest sense.

Had you followed the Surreal Salon in past years? What did you know about it? I had heard about the Surreal Salon through the pop surrealist art community for years, but this was the first time I lived close enough to attend in person. I kept hearing that it felt a little like an unofficial kickoff to Mardi Gras season, that people came in elaborate costumes and that the whole evening had this celebratory, slightly otherworldly atmosphere.

What I did not realize until participating this year was that some people actually design their costumes based on the artwork in the exhibition. That was amazing to see. At one point someone came up to me wearing a costume inspired by my piece, and getting to watch him model it and explain how the sculpture influenced the design completely made my night. It felt like the work had briefly stepped out of the gallery and into the room!

Also, it was a wonderful addition to have SWOON be the juror for this year's contest. I have done it in the past, and it was hard, fulfilling work. What did you know of SWOON's work and did that inform your submission at all? I have admired Swoon’s work for a long time, especially her installations and the way she moves between sculpture, architecture, and public intervention. I first heard about her in 2009 when she brought the Swimming Cities of Serenissima project to the Venice Biennale. A fleet of sculptural rafts floating into one of the most formalized spaces in the art world was such an unforgettable gesture.

The act of arriving that way, without waiting for institutional permission, became part of the artwork itself. That kind of boldness has always stayed with me. It is difficult to break into the art world, especially in spaces where voice is carefully selected and curated. Seeing an artist carve out space for herself so creatively was incredibly inspiring.

I also love the direction her work has been taking recently with the Sibylant Sisters project. My own work is deeply inspired by myth and storytelling, so it has been fascinating to watch her develop that world, creating her own oracle cards and building a living mythology around the work. There is something powerful about artists inventing symbolic languages that people can enter into. So having the chance to meet her and have her encounter one of my installations was a very meaningful moment for me.

You work in a few different mediums, and sculpture and installation seem to be your focus. Talk a little bit about your process and where you feel most comfortable as a maker? I am not sure I feel comfortable in any single medium, and I think that is probably a good thing. I tend to move toward whatever material feels necessary for the idea at hand. In many ways my practice grew out of practical constraints. For a long time I did not have a large studio, so I had to find ways of making work that could expand into a space temporarily and then disappear again. Sand, modular sculptural elements, and ephemeral materials all emerged from that reality.

Over time those limitations became part of the language of the work itself. I am drawn to materials that hold a sense of fragility and transformation. Installation allows me to build an environment around the sculpture where those ideas can unfold more fully, where the viewer is not just looking at an object but stepping into a moment or a story.

What sort of artists influenced you as you began to find your own voice? And, sort of as a nice anecdote, what is the last work that made you stop in your tracks and get back into the studio and create?

Voice is an interesting concept to me as a woman, because women often face particular obstacles when it comes to the emergence of voice. It takes a certain measure of audacity to say something and commit it to art. In a way you are asking the world to listen. Because of that, I am especially inspired by women who make art without asking permission.

I mentioned earlier how powerful it was for me to learn about Swoon bringing her Swimming Cities project to the Venice Biennale. That gesture has always stayed with me, not only because of the work itself but because of the confidence behind it. The willingness to claim space in a world that does not always easily offer it. Moments like that remind me that voice is not only about what you say as an artist, but about allowing yourself to say it at all. That idea continues to shape the way I approach my own work.

As for the last artwork that made me stop in my tracks, I recently visited the Museo Nacional de Antropología in Mexico City. Walking through the galleries of figurative ceramics from different regions of Mexico was completely mesmerizing. The Mayan ceramics in particular took my breath away. There is so much spirit in them, such a sense of presence. I encountered one ceramic face that affected me deeply. I have gone back to see it several times now, and each time I leave feeling more inspired to return to sculpture.

What else do you have lined up this year? Are you someone who likes to work in a gallery situation, or do you prefer alternative means to show your work? This summer I will be working with Raf Gallery in Reykjavik, Iceland during the month of August. A total solar eclipse will pass directly over Reykjavik on August 12, and later that month the city celebrates Menningarnótt, a large citywide festival of arts and culture.

Raf Gallery works with both artwork and Baltic amber jewelry, and I have always been drawn to amber as both a material and a mythological object. For the exhibition I will be installing sculpture and a sand installation that tells the myth of the birth of Baltic amber while also reflecting on eclipse mythology and the relationship between darkness and light.

The sand will come from the local shoreline, and at the end of the exhibition I invite the community to dismantle the installation with me. We carry the sand back to the ocean and return it with a wish, prayer, or intention.

I love Iceland deeply. The black sand I often use in my installations was inspired by the volcanic beach at Reynisfjara, so being able to create work there during such a rare celestial moment feels very meaningful.

As for where I like to show my work, I enjoy many different contexts. My installations have appeared in galleries, museums, empty storefronts, and even city halls. But my favorite place for ephemeral work is the beach.

When I lived near the sea in Washington State, friends and I would sometimes build temporary altars from flowers, driftwood, shells, and plants as offerings to the water. The tide would slowly carry everything away. There is something very special about building something together that only exists for that one night.

What did you like about the whole Surreal Salon experience? What were some of the highlights?The whole evening had an incredible energy. The costumes alone were extraordinary, and everywhere you looked there was another small moment of creativity unfolding. Music, conversation, artists reconnecting, people discovering work for the first time. It felt celebratory in the best way.

There was also an unexpected moment early in the night. Someone accidentally backed into the platform holding my installation, and when the platform shifted the sand vibrated and many of the detailed designs disappeared. Thankfully the person who tripped was completely fine, which was the most important thing. But in a strange way the moment also revealed something essential about the work. Some people had assumed the sand had been glued down or painted in place. When it shifted, it suddenly became clear that the entire surface was loose and hand-drawn. I sat beside the piece and carefully repaired it, re-drawing the patterns into the sand and amber while people watched.

For me that moment captured the spirit of the work. The installation only existed in that exact form on that particular night. It could be recreated, but it would never be exactly the same again. Everyone there was witnessing something temporary, something that belonged only to that moment in time. And in a way that felt very fitting for the Surreal Salon itself.River Reishi is a multidisciplinary artist whose sculptures and ephemeral sand installations explore myth, grief, and the mysterious threshold between worlds. Drawing on feminine water deities and ancient storytelling traditions, she works with materials such as sand, amber, and light to create environments that exist only briefly in time.See more at riverreishi.com and on Instagram @riverreishi.

#9166. Clouds Were Once Photography’s Greatest Challenge

The Met Museum’s “Chasing Clouds” is a pleasing romp through the technical problem of capturing clouds at photography’s beginning.

The original 1996 Windows XP default background is arguably the most viewed photo of all time; its cumulus puffs drifting across a way-too-blue sky are seared into my and countless others’ Y2K childhoods. Such images of fluffy clouds are so ubiquitous that it’s hard to believe they once presented one of photography’s greatest technological challenges. The Met exhibition Chasing Clouds is a pleasing romp through the history of this problem through a union of art and science, spanning the early 1800s to 1929 — roughly photography’s first century. While the medium showed promise as “the pencil of nature,” its first processes were overly sensitive to blue light, registering the sky as a blank white space, impossibly overexposed.

While this lent some images a minimalist mystique, like John Beasley Greene’s “The Nile in Front of the Theban Hills” (1853–54), other photographers resorted to painting clouds into their landscapes by hand. An initial breakthrough came when French photographer Gustave Le Gray figured out how to stitch together two pictures — one calibrated to sky, and the other to land and sea. (Photographic fakery is as old as the medium itself.)

Though the exhibition begins with painted cloud studies and ends with photographic modernism, visual discoveries unfold in a dialogue between painting and technology rather than as a scientific march from one to the other. This makes for a much more interesting story; obsolescence is often a capitalist public relations trick.

#9165. Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality

“The crisis is the system that we’re in,” the Pulitzer Prize-winning data journalist and artist says in an interview with Hyperallergic about her first book, “Ten Lives.”

“As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Known best for her indelible data visualizations, from the obscenity of Jeff Bezos’s wealth to the Israeli government’s starvation of Palestinians in Gaza and the racial and gender biases in museum collections, the Pulitzer Prize-winning Iraqi-British journalist tackles the subject of wealth and economic inequality in America in her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026).

When I met her in the West Village in September, she’d just come from recording its accompanying audiobook, a delicate process given the visuals on its pages. Chalabi organized meticulous interviews conducted with anonymous subjects across income levels over the course of six years into 10 vividly fleshed-out characters. Each represents a particular economic class, illustrated in her signature hand-drawn style and punctuated by reflections on her own financial struggles as a young journalist and, more recently, in the wake of her mother’s illness. Chalabi carries a long tradition of data visualization — W.E.B. Du Bois’s The Exhibit of American Negroes comes to mind — into her refreshing candor about class and the stifling silence around it, particularly in journalism and the art world.

That insistence on specificity and honesty in her reporting goes hand-in-hand with her political advocacy; Chalabi donated her $15,000 Pulitzer Prize award to the Palestinian Journalists Syndicate and has been fighting for Palestinian rights since she was a teenager. Her drive to seek out and represent truth, in Ten Lives and in her social media posts, is anchored in a sensitivity and profound sense of responsibility. In this way, she restores some of the humanity and dignity to the statistics that capture the brutality of genocide, exploitation, and economic inequality, one brushstroke at a time. In an interview, we spoke about the financial realities of journalism, the value of collaboration in an era of isolation, and the art and literature that sustains her. Our conversation has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

Hyperallergic: In the intro to Ten Lives, you recall getting scolded for not observing “the etiquette of looking away” as a child. And it’s so striking that you have made a career of doing the opposite. How did you decide to make class, something we’re taught to overlook from a young age, the subject of this book?

Mona Chalabi: The first line of the original manuscript said, “I wrote this book because I was paid a shitload of money to write it.”

#9164. Kohei Yamada: MY SCREEN TESTS @ Gr Gallery, New York (UPDATED with Installation Imagery)

GR gallery is pleased to present My Screen Tests, the first New York City solo exhibition by Kohei Yamada. The exhibition examines the enduring value of the authentic relationship between artist and artwork, engaging in themes of irony, introspection, and visual metaphor, which draw inspiration from contemporary practice and Yamada’s nuanced admiration for American Pop art.

Presenting a new suite of paintings on canvas -each paired with its esquisse on paper- In My Screen Tests, Yamada searches within New York City’s identity as the art capital of the world in order to infuse his work with a distinct vitality, revealing his admiration for Andy Warhol through motifs referencing the Silver Factory era and its entourage, and evoking tension between a sense of historical prestige and vibrant pop expressions. This interplay initiates a critical conversation between perceptions of art and is worthwhile in examining the creative directions of today’s world.

My Screen Tests is defined by motivations that comment on the ambiguous nature of art’s true value beyond its creator, while also alluding to Yamada’s need to remain bound to art for the rest of his life. The work also critiques the world’s normalization of deceit and capitalistic greed, alongside a persistent

longing for freedom that remains just out of reach. New York City lies at the core of Yamada’s practice, serving as both subject and catalyst for exploring the interplay between personal perception and nostalgia. It also functions as a cultural bridge between American and Japanese influences, tracing the artist’s journey from childhood through his engagement with the legacy of Andy Warhol, as well as other Japanese and American artists. Through a combination of brushwork, abstraction, and figuration, Yamada weaves a narrative rich in contemporary art history, while also confronting the true value of an artist’s existence.

Over half of the works exclusively made for My Screen Tests are imbued with references inspired by Warhol’s practice and artistic values, cast against New York City as a hub for experimentation where art meets and even challenges commerce. Repetition and humor are also at the core of the artist’s creative process, adding a wittiness and discipline to his work, while also connecting it on a deeper level to the Pop tradition. Yamada draws upon the city as both muse and stage, invoking a range of artistic influences as main characters, while ultimately revealing each to be a projection of his own identity.

The opening reception will take place on Friday, May 15 from 6:00 pm to 8:00 pm. The artist will participate in the opening reception.

#9163. Mona Chalabi on Money and Art

An interview with the Pulitzer Prize winner, Lori Waxman on bringing sexy back in Chicago, stolen Picasso prints found, and the problem with clouds.

“I wrote this book because I was paid a shitload of money to write it,” Mona Chalabi says in her new book Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are — or tried to, anyway, before her editor stopped her. The Iraqi-British, Pulitzer-winning artist and illustrator has made a career saying what nobody else can, or will — calling out fellow journalists for their refusal to report on Palestine, for instance. Today, she talks to Associate Editor Laskhmi Rivera Amin about her data-driven, hand-drawn process, as well as how class and inequality shape journalism, art, and our lives.

Funny — as an editor, my favorite thing is not stopping my writers. That’s precisely how Lori Waxman’s piece on the return of sexy art in Chicago was born. No, this is not a personal essay about her or her acquaintances’ sexuality (“Maybe after everyone’s dead,” she says). It’s much better — loaded with art historical judgments (has anyone referred to Willem de Kooning’s drawings as “slasher sketches” before? We ought to); discussion of glory holes and sexy architecture; and gems about life (“female middle-age libido sets at either zero or 1,000, on a scale of one to 100”). God, I love my job.

#9162. How Miles Greenberg Got “WAR” Past the Censors

“There was not a single outlet, institution, or gallery that wanted to get behind this thing,” the artist told Hyperallergic about his new, six-hour performance piece.

Miles Greenberg’s mother took him to see Marina Abramović perform The Artist Is Present at the Museum of Modern Art when he was just 12 years old. The experience would serve as the zero point for the New York-based Canadian artist’s own performance-based practice, and the birth of his unyielding desire to “see [his] work at a museum, where it would be approached as a sculpture.” Later training under playwright Robert Wilson, choreographer Édouard Lock, and the very “grandmother of performance art” who spurred his interest in the medium, Greenberg began developing works that ironically share more with the histories of painting and sculpture than a lineage of performance. He has stood on plinths as the tortured satyr Marsyas from Greek mythology, the arrow-pierced Christian martyr Saint Sebastian, and in original statuesque poses that recall the Baroque ecstasy of a Bernini sculpture.

On October 29, the artist presented “WAR” (2026), a six-hour durational performance organized by Performa and curated by Zoe Lukov. More than 40 performers walked on treadmills in the vacant site of the former 86th Street Cinema in New York to a trance-like score by artist Chino Amobi. Greenberg spoke with Hyperallergic about the difficulties of securing a venue for the work amid Israel's genocide on Palestine, the limitations of endurance, and performance as a “gateway into a state that is difficult to reach.”

Hyperallergic: You often reference martyrs, saints, warriors, and other archetypes across history dedicated to either heroic causes or beliefs beyond themselves. Why are you interested in these figures? Do they resonate with you besides their art-historical or imagistic qualities?

Miles Greenberg: The West has canonized these stories as a means of cutting right to a series of moralistic teachings that have been central to Western societies writ large for the last several millennia. They're represented in different ways, but there's this longstanding tradition of just about every artist from the Renaissance up until contemporary times — though, maybe to a lesser extent — regurgitating these art-historical figures, characters, stories, and fables over and over again.

With performance, which continues to be niche and sit around the edges of art history, people’s minds go more to the shock value of it, which I’m not particularly seduced or interested by, rather than what it is that we mean or wish to convey. So it’s really a strategic play on my behalf to choreograph or rein in their imagination and channel it in the right direction. I think of these works as portraits more than I wish to identify with the figures. There can be some crossover. Saint Sebastian is a notable example I have some personal investment in as a queer person.

I also think situating myself centrally in that tradition helps to quite simply attribute value and clarity and define my practice within that canon and lineage of art history, rather than somehow adjacent or parallel to it as a young queer Black performance-based person. I’m not interested in marginality as a destination, and I don’t see any reason not to put me in conversation with the canon. I was raised by the canon, so I’m going to make like the canon.

H: What led you to turn to the subject of war with this particular work?

Christmas is coming, which means annoying music in shops, an inevitable lack of snow, and Kim Kardashian charging $148 for the contents of her bathroom drawer.

Kim's 'SKIMS Accessories Advent Calendar' has achieved that rare festive miracle: making a chocolate-based advent calendar look like a sound financial investment. Because what we have here, for a cool $148/£158, is twelve days of tat. Hair ties. Scrunchies. Bobby pins. Keychains. A squishy toy. Something called a 'bra elastic headband'. It's essentially the contents of a lost property box.

Unsurprisingly, the internet is having a field day. A viral TikTok unboxing has attracted tens of millions of views, with its creator becoming visibly more exasperated as each compartment reveals another object you could reasonably expect to find down the back of a sofa, culminating in the grand finale: a furry compact mirror keychain.

It's worth saying that from a branding packaging design perspective, it's almost impressive. It's a nice-looking object with pretty illustrations, and the SKIMS wordmark is striking in a bold, festive red. But there's something beautifully 2026 about taking a handful of mundane objects, putting them in expensive-looking packaging and asking people to cough up the cost of an actual spa day. Like so many of this year's main characters (AI, subscription-based everything, $10 matcha lattes), it's overpriced, overhyped and underwhelming. But unlike AI, that $148 leaving your bank account definitely isn't artificial.

In response to the backlash, SKIMS has emailed customers who purchased the advent calendar: “We wanted to reach out personally about your recent purchase of the Holiday 2026 advent calendar. We understand the product did not meet customers’ expectations, and we are truly sorry. We want every customer to be happy with what they receive, and we fell short this time.”

Believe it or not, this isn't the first time we've seen a celebrity's brand take a hit as a result of an underwhelming advent calendar. Back in 2017, popular vlogger Zoella faced backlash for her own calendar. Like Kim's it contained only twelve doors, all of which were filled with items that might be found down the back of a sofa. Unlike Kim's, it was a mere $60. Inflation, eh?

#9160. Prize dedicated to African women artists expands to Senegal, announces 2026 winners

Centre: Fatoumata Sy and Kwama Frigaux’s uncle Mr. Pacx, representing the artist at the award ceremony. LEft prize jury members Dominique Heyse-Moore, Touria El- Glaoui, Alexa Waley-Cohen. Right: Leila Zakhem, the prize director and Valerie Lesbros, the director of the Institut Francis du Sénégal

The Ghanaian-French artist Kwama Frigaux and the Senegalese Fatoumata Sy have been announced as the joint winners of the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize. The prize, founded by the London and Accra-based Gallery 1957 in 2021 to support women artists in Ghana and its diaspora, has this year expanded to include artists from Senegal, in partnership with Institut Français du Sénégal. Frigaux and Fatoumata have been awarded $5,000 each, as well as a three-month residency (in Senegal for the Ghanaian and in Ghana for the Senegalese), and solo exhibitions.

The prize is named after the former Ashanti queen mother, renowned for her anticolonial resistance at a time when Ghana was under British rule. The call for applications for this year’s edition opened in June and ran until September, and was open to Ghanaian and Senegalese women artists aged 18 or older, based either in their home countries or in the diaspora. The winners were announced during Accra Cultural Week (29 October -2 November), which is organised by Gallery 1957. On view there until 5 December 2026 is The Lore of Care: Maternal Acts of Devotion, a solo show by Theresah Ankomah, the winner of the 2025 Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize.

Installation view of The Lore of Care: Maternal Acts of Devotion, a show of work by the 2025 Yaa Asantewaa Prize winner Theresah Ankomah at 1957 Gallery

Frigaux and Sy were selected by a jury comprising Touria El Glaoui, the founder of the 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair; the Ghanaian artist Serge Attukwei Clottey; Marie Hélène Pereira, a senior curator at Berlin’s Haus der Kulturen der Welt; Jeanne Barral, a curator at the Fondation Cartier; the collector Alexa Waley-Cohen; and Dominique Heyse-Moore, the senior curator of contemporary British art at Tate Britain.

Runners up of the prize participate in a mentorship programme, which provides support on topics such as grant applications and entrepreneurship. Mentors this year include the Nigerian artist Modupeola Fadugba and Aisha Ayensu, the founder of the Ghanaian luxury fashion brand Christie Brown.

"I think [it's] an incredible programme that helps drive the longevity of [the prize's] impact,” Leila Zakhem, the director of the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize, tells The Art Newspaper. “And it really creates a beautiful community.”

Zakhem explains that her team considered several countries for the expansion, including Nigeria. A key part of this search was finding a "very good implementing partner." The Institut Français du Sénégal, which is "a non-commercial space [has] a lot of credibility,” she adds, “and they were very excited to partner with us on the prize.” Zakhem says that she hopes the expansion will help develop and create a bridge between art communities in English- and French-speaking West Africa.

The planned next steps for the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize are to expand further into West Africa, and then potentially beyond, with winners selected from different regions of the continent. “The goal is eventually to be the leading Pan-African female art prize on the continent,” Zakhem says.

Accra-based Gallery 1957 organises prize to celebrate its fifth birthday, with all-star jury set to announce cash prizes for three winners

The new prize, which includes $5000 and a residency in Benin City, was open to artists living in Ghana and Nigeria

#9159. Fall 2026 Art and Architecture Books from Yale University Press

The Bayeux tapestry, a new biography of Edward Hopper, The Met's exhibition catalogue on Krasner and Pollock, what architecture is, and more

The Fall 2026 lineup of art and architecture books from Yale University Press has both beauty and erudition. Exhibition catalogues from our museum publishing partners include Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous (The Metropolitan Museum of Art), Mary Cassatt: After Impressionism (Art Institute of Chicago), Roy Lichtenstein: Like New (Whitney Museum of American Art), and The Bayeux Tapestry (British Museum).

Owen Davies explores the Art of Divination across time and geography; Witold Rybczynski is characteristically eloquent on What Architecture Is; Neil Levine analyzes The Sculpture of Donald Judd; and Louis Shadwick gives us a brilliant new biography of Edward Hopper.

In this captivating book, Owen Davies explores the global history of divination practices from tea leaves and tarot cards to pyromancy and palmistry that seek to answer questions that range from the philosophical and metaphysical to the romantic and personal. Organized into six thematic groups—observing the natural world; making patterns; communicating with gods and spirits; signs from the human body and mind; looking to the heavens; and chance and calculation—Art of Divination allows readers to see connections between different ages and places.

The Bayeux Tapestry is an iconic artwork, almost seventy meters long, which tells the story of the events leading to the Norman Conquest of England in 1066 by William, Duke of Normandy. Featuring a full-color reproduction of the Tapestry and all-new photography, this beautiful book allows the reader to follow the visual narrative—with a scene-by-scene transliteration and English translation of the Tapestry’s Latin—while texts from international experts unpick the importance of the work in understanding this pivotal point in European history.

The book surveys two icons of Abstract Expressionism that examines their distinct but connected careers and artistic legacies.

By Louis ShadwickEdward Hopper: A Life reexamines the standard view of this renowned artist by interweaving his life and work and vividly reconstructing the personal, cultural, historical, and political contexts of his time. Using major new archives and a wealth of newly discovered sources, Louis Shadwick presents the richest and most complete story of Hopper’s life and art to date, revealing new dimensions to an artist whose carefully wrought identity has never been fully unraveled.

Mary Cassatt (1844–1926) was a trailblazing artist who worked across media, manipulated materials, transformed subjects through series and scale, and marketed and exhibited her artwork in novel ways. In Mary Cassatt: After Impressionism, scholars highlight Cassatt’s daring, ingenuity, and ceaselessly independent vision—both in her artistic technique and choice of subject matter—and consider the lasting impact of her aesthetic breakthroughs and significant legacy.

By Alex Da Corte and Meg OnliContributions by Dan Nadel, Marshall N Price and Carmen Winant

A career-spanning look at the methods, influences, motivations, and continuing relevance of one of America’s foremost Pop artists.

The Sculpture of Donald Judd is the first chronological study of the artist’s pathbreaking and enormously influential work beginning with his turn from painting to sculpture in 1961–62 until his death in 1994. The analyses of the work, often considered the foundation of Minimalism, are based on close readings, highly attentive to detail and informed by a friendship with the artist.

This residency at the U-M Stamps School, in partnership with the U-M Museum of Art (UMMA), offers artists a $20,000 honorarium, housing, studio space, and a culminating exhibition in UMMA’s prominent Stenn Gallery.

Funding for tuition, healthcare, and stipends is available. Apply to the University of Maryland, Baltimore County program by Feb 1 to be considered for financial support.

Generously funded, renowned faculty and visiting artists, spacious studios, and an exhibition at the Manetti Shrem Museum of Art.

Picture this: You've been grinding toward your FI number, optimizing every dollar, and you've accumulated a stash of Chase Ultimate Rewards points sitting in your account. Now imagine checking into a clean, comfortable Hyatt Place in a city you're visiting for a wedding, a family reunion, or a long weekend — and the front desk agent hands you your keycard while your account balance drops by exactly 5,000 points. Not $150. Not $180. Five thousand points that you earned by buying groceries. That's the Category 1 Hyatt sweet spot — and it's the single most accessible, repeatable, high-value redemption in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A standard night at a Hyatt Place or Hyatt House in a mid-size U.S. city routinely runs **$100–$200 per night** in cash. At 5,000 points per night, you're redeeming at **2–4 cents per point (CPP)** — a range that demolishes the standard 1 cent per point benchmark that most casual rewards users never surpass. At 4 CPP on a $200 night, you're getting four times the value of a simple cash-back card. Every. Single. Time. The pricing inefficiency here is structural, not accidental. World of Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** — meaning a Category 1 property costs 5,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in January or a Friday night during a sold-out college football weekend when cash rates are spiking. The loyalty program doesn't dynamically price awards the way airlines do. That fixed ceiling is your edge. For the ChooseFI community, this redemption isn't just good — it's foundational. It's the first sweet spot that proves the system works. Before you're ready to redeem 60,000 points for a business class flight to Tokyo, you need to feel what it's like to hand over a handful of points and walk into a hotel room that would have cost you real money. This is that moment. It builds the muscle memory, the confidence, and the conviction that travel rewards are real — and that you're playing the game correctly. This is where the journey starts.

World of Hyatt consistently delivers the highest cents-per-point value of any major hotel loyalty program. While Hilton and Marriott have moved to dynamic pricing — where award costs fluctuate based on demand — Hyatt maintains a fixed award chart. This structural difference is your edge. A Category 1 property costs 5,000 points whether it is a quiet Tuesday in February or a sold-out homecoming weekend. Combined with Chase Ultimate Rewards transfer ratios (1:1 from Sapphire Reserve, 4:3 from Sapphire Preferred) and instant transfer speed, Hyatt redemptions are the single best use of UR points for hotel stays. The ChooseFI community considers this the entry point that proves the entire travel rewards system works.

The core insight behind this sweet spot is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt uses a fixed-price award chart, and Category 1 is priced at a floor that hasn't kept pace with rising hotel cash rates.

Most hotel loyalty programs have moved to dynamic pricing — meaning award nights fluctuate with demand, just like cash rates. Marriott Bonvoy, Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards — they've all largely eliminated fixed charts in favor of algorithms that squeeze more points out of you when demand is high. Hyatt has held the line on a fixed chart, and that stubbornness is your opportunity.

The Category 1 floor sits at 5,000 points per night. As cash rates for qualifying properties have climbed with inflation — many now regularly pricing at $150–$200+ — the points cost has remained anchored. The gap between what the market charges and what Hyatt charges in points is widening in your favor every year. That's not a bug in the system. It's a feature you're uniquely positioned to exploit by understanding it.

This redemption is built on two of the best transferable points currencies available to everyday consumers:

Both transfers are instant, which means you can search for availability before committing your points, confirm the room you want is bookable, and then initiate the transfer and complete the booking — all in one sitting. This is a critical distinction from some airline partners where transfers take 24–72 hours and you're transferring on faith. With Hyatt, there's no leap of faith required.

The transfer ratio matters. With a Sapphire Reserve, every UR point becomes one Hyatt point — 15,000 UR points covers three Category 1 nights with zero waste. With a Sapphire Preferred, the 4:3 ratio means you need 20,000 UR points for the same 15,000 Hyatt points. Bilt transfers at 1:1.

World of Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award bookings. This matters more for higher-tier redemptions, but it's worth internalizing as a feature of the program overall. When you book 5,000 points for a hotel night, that's your cost. You'll pay any applicable taxes at checkout — typically $10–$25 — but there are no program-imposed carrier fees or redemption surcharges eating into your value.

Hyatt's full chart runs from 3,500 points (Category 1 standard) up to 45,000 points (Category 8) per night. Understanding this structure helps you see the Category 1 sweet spot in context: it's the entry point, but it's not a consolation prize. Hyatt Place and Hyatt House properties are upper-midscale hotels — clean, well-maintained, often with free breakfast at Hyatt House locations and complimentary parking in suburban markets. These aren't budget motels. You're getting a genuinely comfortable night's sleep for points that most people have already earned without trying.

Booking a Category 1 Hyatt award is one of the smoothest processes in all of travel rewards. Here's exactly how to do it from start to finish.

Before anything else, log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account at chase.com/ultimaterewards or your Bilt Rewards account at biltrewards.com and confirm your current points balance. You need a minimum of 5,000 points per night to execute this redemption. If you have 15,000 points, you can book up to three nights.

Go to hyatt.com and log in or create a free World of Hyatt account (it's free to join). Use the search bar to enter your destination city and travel dates. Once results populate, filter by "Points" or "Use Points" using the toggle at the top of the results page. This will display the award rate alongside the cash rate for every property.

Filter further by selecting "Category 1–2" under the Points filter to quickly surface the lowest-cost options. Availability is typically strong — Hyatt.com shows real-time award inventory, and Category 1 properties almost always have rooms open. The booking window extends 395 days out, so you can plan well in advance for travel around a specific event.

Once you've found the property and dates you want, note the exact points cost displayed. For Category 1 properties, this should read 5,000 points per night. Add the room to your cart and proceed — but do not check out yet if your Hyatt account currently has zero balance.

Open a new browser tab and navigate to your Chase Ultimate Rewards portal (chase.com/ultimaterewards) or Bilt dashboard. Select "Transfer to Travel Partners" and choose World of Hyatt from the list. Enter the number of points you need (5,000 per night, minimum), confirm your World of Hyatt membership number, and initiate the transfer.

Chase and Bilt transfers to Hyatt are instant. Note: Sapphire Reserve transfers at 1:1 while Sapphire Preferred transfers at 4:3 (4 UR = 3 Hyatt). Refresh your Hyatt account and your points will be there, ready to use.

Return to your Hyatt browser tab and complete the checkout process. Select "Redeem Points" as your payment method, confirm the points deduction matches what you expected, and finalize the reservation. You'll receive a confirmation email immediately.

You transferred 10,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points from your Sapphire Reserve to World of Hyatt last week (it took about 30 seconds, and at 1:1 every point landed). Your Hyatt account shows a 10,000-point balance. You complete the booking, pay the ~$30 in taxes at checkout, and you're done.

That's more than three times the value most people extract from their points programs. And those 10,000 Chase UR points? You earned them by putting your regular monthly spending on your Chase Sapphire card for a few months.

At the Hyatt Place, you'll check into a well-appointed room with a king bed, a sofa sleating area, and a bathroom that doesn't make you feel like you're in a budget motel. Hyatt House properties (also frequently Category 1 or 2) often include a complimentary hot breakfast — eggs, waffles, fruit — served every morning. In some suburban markets, these properties also offer free parking, turning your 5,000-point night into an even stronger value play when you factor in parking rates that might otherwise run $20–$30/night.

This isn't a flashy Park Hyatt penthouse suite. But it's a genuinely comfortable, predictably high-quality stay that you've effectively taken off your cash budget — freeing that $338 for experiences, food, or your investment accounts. That's the ChooseFI mindset applied to travel.

Stack your Hyatt Globalist benefits if you qualify. If you hold World of Hyatt's top elite status (Globalist, earned at 60 qualifying nights), you receive complimentary breakfast at most full-service properties and room upgrades. Even on a 5,000-point award night, your elite benefits apply. That free breakfast alone can add $25–$35 of value to every morning.

Use the Hyatt free night award from the World of Hyatt Credit Card. The World of Hyatt Credit Card (issued by Chase) comes with an annual free night certificate valid at Category 1–4 properties. Book as far out as you can. The Hyatt booking window opens 395 days in advance. For peak travel periods — summer weekends, holiday weekends, major events — inventory at Category 1 properties can thin out. Getting in early locks your room and your rate.

Target Hyatt House properties for family trips. Hyatt House locations frequently feature suite-style rooms with full kitchens, separate living areas, and free hot breakfast included for all guests. A family of four can stay comfortably for 5,000–8,000 points and skip the cost of restaurant breakfasts entirely.

Earn points on the Bilt card on Rent Day. Bilt Rewards runs a bonus promotion on the first of each month — transferring points earned that day at elevated rates. Accumulating Bilt points through rent payments (no transaction fee) is one of the most efficient ways to build a Hyatt balance.

Don't transfer points speculatively. Even though Chase and Bilt transfers to Hyatt are instant, always confirm your specific dates show award availability before transferring. Points transferred to Hyatt cannot be moved back.

Don't ignore the expiration policy. World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. A single qualifying activity — a points transfer, a stay, a credit card purchase — resets the clock. Set a calendar reminder annually to ensure you don't lose your balance.

Don't overlook Category 2 properties. At 8,000 points per night, Category 2 Hyatts often include urban full-service hotels that provide dramatically more value than the jump in points cost suggests. Once you're comfortable with Category 1 redemptions, explore Category 2 as a natural next step.
