Make precise cuts in wood, acrylic and metal with our pick of the best CNC machines.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The best CNC machines let you make precise, repeatable cuts in metal, wood and other materials right from your desk, and we think it's the start of a revolution in small business crafting. The latest generation of desktop CNC machines are typically enclosed, work quietly, and are automated enough that you don't need to be a trained machinist to use them.

They do cost a fair few bob, starting at $1,199 but venturing into the $5000 territory, so they aren't craft machines for the people at this stage.

CNC machines work in the opposite way to the best 3D printers or the best UV machines. Rather than building an object up layer by layer, they carve it out of a solid block with a spinning cutter. That means you can create strong, precise parts in metal, wood and stone, built to last.

I've picked the best CNC machines available to consumers today, along with two promising Kickstarter models that we're excited to see materialise.

Makera launched as a company in 2019, with the aim of lowering the cost of precision desktop manufacturing. Two years later they made a big splash with their first CNC machine, Carvera, which debuted on Kickstarter and is still popular today: we've put it as number two on our list. But the Z1, which launched in 2025, again on Kickstarter, has shaken up the market by driving the cost of entry even lower.

Despite being the cheapest on this list, it does everything a beginner will need. It's built on a cast aluminium frame and fully enclosed. It offers automatic probing and levelling, a built-in camera you can connect to your phone, and an air blast that clears chips as it cuts. And its software offers one-click toolpaths, so you don't need to learn complex software before you get started.

The tradeoff for the cheap price is that it's more limited in terms of size and power. The 200 x 200mm work area also means you can only work with small parts, while the 150W spindle requires shallow, patient passes in metal. Another drawback compared to the Carvera is that you'll need to change tools by hand via a quick-release lever.

If you're seeking your first CNC machine, though, this is our top pick.

The Carvera has been around since 2021 but remains Makera's flagship. With this CNC machine you get a six-slot automatic tool changer, letting you swap between different milling bits mid-job, saving you from having to fiddle about with your hands. It's capable of cutting and milling wood, plastics, acrylics, carbon fiber, FR4 (PCBs) and non-ferrous metals like aluminum and brass.

Other features include an automated wireless probe for surface mapping and bed leveling, built-in dust collection and a 2.5W laser for engraving and engraving and PCB labelling. The enclosed design keeps noise to around 65dB: not silent, but still quiet for a CNC. You can cut wood, plastics, PCBs and non-ferrous metals like aluminium and brass well, and if you want to make circuit boards at home, Makera will sell you a dedicated bundle for that.

The 200W spindle is modest, and Makera doesn't recommend you try to cut steel or titanium. And while the crowdfunded rivals below promise more power at a similar price, remember that they're not actually available yet. This is, and has years of independent tests and positive customer reviews behind it.

Twotrees produces affordable laser engravers and 3D printers, and the ED1 is its latest CNC machine. It offers automatic tool changing, like the Carvera above, but at a more affordable price.

While the ED1 is closer to shipping that the CNC machines below, it's only available for pre-orders, which will ship from January 2027. That means it hasn't yet been independently tested, so at this stage we can only go on the specs.

They do, though, look very impressive. The five-slot changer is said to swap cutters in around 10 seconds, the 600W spindle has three times the power of the Carvera's – Titanium is on its list of materials – and the 300 x 200mm work area is a decent size. You'll also get auto levelling, a built-in camera and AI-assisted software.

These CNC machines haven't shipped yet, so we haven't included them in our main list. Both are due to arrive in early 2027, though, so assuming all goes well, they're well worth keeping an eye on.

Infimaker was founded in Shenzhen in 2024 by former DJI engineers, and the K1 is not just its CNC machine but its first product at all. The Kickstarter closed in September, but late pledges are still open, with delivery estimated for February.

So what's different about this one? Well, most desktop CNC machines are 3-axis: the cutter moves left and right, back and forth, and up and down. This adds two more axes: tilting and rotating the workpiece as it cuts, which allows you carve complex shapes like impellers and sculptures in a single setup, rather than having to re-clamp the part by hand.

This CNC machine features a 1.5kW spindle, a six-tool automatic changer and AI-assisted software. Be aware, though, that you'll need a strong desk, as this weighs a hefty 110kg.

The Tooldance X1 is a crowdfunded CNC machine with a 1.5kW permanent-magnet spindle that aims to deliver high torque at low speeds, enabling you to work with stainless steel and titanium. It promises the largest work area on this list at 400 x 265 x 180mm, along a nine-slot automatic tool changer that uses RFID tags to track its cutters, and sensors that measure your stock for you.

The Kickstarter is still live, with delivery estimated for March 2027. So as you'd expect, there've been no independent tests yet. If you're in the US, also note that the spindle's output drops to around 1kW on a 120V supply.

CNC machines and 3D printers work in opposite ways. A 3D printer is additive: you build up objects up layer by layer, usually from plastic. A CNC machine, in contrast, is subtractive. You begin with a solid block of material and it carves sections away with a spinning cutter.

If you want to make parts from wood, aluminium, brass and even steel, a CNC machine is a better choice than a 3D printer. You'll typically get a stronger, smoother finish than most 3D prints. Be aware, though, that it's much more difficult to make hollow or enclosed shapes than with a 3D printer.

A 3-axis machine moves the cutter left and right, forwards and back, and up and down. This is usually all you need for flat parts, signs and reliefs. With 4-axis machine, you also get a rotary attachment that turns the workpiece. This allows you you to carve around cylinders. A 5-axis machine adds the option to tilt the part, so the cutter can reach almost any angle in one setup. This makes it easier to make complex shapes.

#9058. Tesla "winding down" production of Cybertruck

According to a recent tweet by Tesla founder Elon Musk, the electric vehicle company will be decreasing production of the Cybertruck at its Texas Gigafactory, just two and a half years after the car’s debut.

Musk said on Friday morning that Cybertruck production will be “winding down” to “make room” for the Cybercab, an electric sedan Tesla unveiled in 2024.

The change will go into effect starting mid-2027, according to Musk. It is unclear if the Cybertruck will be completely discontinued, although Musk agreed with a user of Musk-owned social media platform X, who called the news an “end of an era”.

“True, but the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time”, the Tesla founder replied.

Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production

The Texas Gigafactory outside of Austin is the only factory known to produce the Cybertruck, according to MSN.

The shift may be due to poor sales of the vehicle since it was delivered to customers starting in late 2023.

The company sold 20, 237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024, representing a 48 per cent drop, according to an estimate from Kelley Blue Book.

Musk estimated the company would sell an average of between 250,000 and 500,000 trucks annually at a 2023 shareholders’ meeting.

The Cybertruck design was first unveiled in 2019. It quickly divided opinion for its boxy shape and sci-fi appearance.

It was launched and placed in showrooms in 2023. Shortly after, many models were recalled in 2024 due to faulty pedals.

Tesla has been shifting its factory lines in recent years, seemingly to usher in the production of its semi-autonomous products.

One example is the Cybercab due to be folded into the company’s robotaxi service.

Earlier this year, Tesla announced it shifted production lines for its Model S and Model X vehicles into fabrication of its Optimus humanoid robot, which recently went into production in California.

The company also debuted a flying Roadster concept car to much fanfare last month.

I tested these two retro-gaming watches, and one of them made me ridiculously happy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mega Man is the better game, but Space Invaders is the better watch to wear. Both My Play Watch models cost around $79.99 / £79.99 and do the same basics: time, calendar, stopwatch and calculator. Neither has notifications.

Space Invaders was the first game I ever played, or at least the first I can remember playing. I played it on a black-and-white CRT with an Atari 2600 (which is why I loved the Atari 2600+), crouched cross-legged on the floor, my face pressed against the TV screen. Our local swimming pool had an arcade because, back then, game cabinets appeared everywhere, but it was off-limits to me at eight.

I’m an adult now, so I can have Space Invaders, which remained one of the best games of the 80s after its release in 1978, on my wrist and play it whenever I like. In colour, too. That’s the pitch behind the My Play Watch series, which brings retro game brands back as digital watches. (For more, check out the indie game aping the visual design of old LCD game and watch gadgets.)

The Mega Man-branded My Play Watch is a different story. I came to the series late, on PlayStation, but of the two, this is arguably the watch with the more interesting game. It’s a reworked version of Mega Man 2, playable on a tiny watch face. Mega Man runs automatically; tap and hold the screen to jump, then release to fire, and beating bosses unlocks new watch faces.

+ It’s Mega Man 2 reworked+ Multiple watch faces- It isn’t a straight portBuilt on a renewed version of Mega Man 2 designed to be played on a watch face, this is arguably the better watch, but I just don't connect with Capcom's icon in the same way as Space Invaders…

+ Arcade sounds and art+ Gamified health stats - The game is very simple… And this is why the 1980-inspired Space Invaders smartwatch, in limited-edition yellow, is my preferred pick. It may not be as experimental as Mega Man, but it's my nostalgia pill.

The blue retro watch and game capture the feel of Mega Man 2 despite the simplified controls, and the bosses and music are still there, bleeping away on my wrist. It isn’t a straight port, though. There are no Robot Master weapons, some enemies and minibosses are missing, and the levels have been changed. Controls can get fiddly when your finger covers the screen.

And yet I’ve kept Space Invaders on my wrist, even though its version of the game is simple. You move the little ship left and right using the side dial and tap the screen to fire. Sure, it's not as easy as playing on one of the best retro game consoles like the new Evercade Nexus, but look how tiny it is. It’s easy to pick up but hard to play while wearing, and the original arcade sounds and pixel-art watch faces sell the nostalgia, even if anyone nearby will tut and raise an irksome eyebrow at the loud bleeps and famously high-pitched 'pew-cssssh' as an Invader turns to pixel dust.

Nostalgia and collectibility are what sell these watches, and they’ve sold me. I love looking down and seeing the little animated Space Invader pixel monster waving back at me, or the bright original cabinet art sat on my wrist.

But they also have to do more than simply callback to my childhood, and that’s where both watches have a smart retro design. The smartest touch is the health tracking. Step count, calories, and heart rate turn into gamified stats, with my daily rates shown right next to my Space Invaders high score. It’s a small thing, but it makes checking my wrist and health updates feel like celebrating a scoreboard.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Elsewhere, these watches do what a digital watch needs to do in 2026: show the time, a calendar, a stopwatch and a calculator, but they have no notifications or advanced smartwatch features, which is either refreshing and on-brand for a retro game and watch, or a lack of digital detail. Personally, I’m happy to not have WhatsApps buzzing every 10 minutes. The design is a nice touch, too. Both use UI and fonts inspired by their games, and Space Invaders makes stellar use of pixel-art digits that take me straight back to 1982. The strap is spray-painted with Invaders, too (and each watch includes an alternative strap if you want to tone down the retro branding).

Just keep your expectations in check. This collectable tells the time, not an Apple Watch or Garmin rival. No notifications, a small screen not built for long play sessions but designed to take you back to simpler times and scratch that collectables itch – new editions include Street Fighter 2 and a gloriously obnoxious glowing green and pink Centipede edition that I kind of want for no apparent reason but mostly because these things become a container for our emotions.

At around $79.99 / £79.99, Mega Man is the better game, but Space Invaders is the one I’ve kept on, because, like all things retro, it’s completely personal.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

#9056. How to Calculate Your Rising and Moon Sign: A Beginner’s Guide

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “big three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the big three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the big three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina says.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she says.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach new situations in life.”

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is important here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

“Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina says.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina says.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina says it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most important planet in your chart.

“It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she says it just represents overall traits.

Verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she says.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

“The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina says.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is important, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

To find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

#9055. This week Kengo Kuma unveiled a pyramidal brick bathhouse

This week on Dezeen Japanese designer Kengo Kuma’s Kai Water Culture House, which features pyramidal towers, was revealed nearing completion in Copenhagen.

The 5,800-square-metre aquatic centre on the city’s harbour will contain 10 indoor and outdoor pools and is opening next month. Kuma designed the project alongside Danish firms Cornelius Vöge, Søren Jensen and Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects.

In Sydney, museum Powerhouse Parramatta opens today. Designed by architecture studios Moreau Kusunoki and Genton, it is described as the largest cultural project in Australia since the Sydney Opera House.

Powerhouse Parramatta is located on the banks of the Parramatta River in western Sydney and wrapped by a steel-lattice exoskeleton.

Annual design week Designart Tokyo is currently taking place in venues across the Japanese capital. Among six standout projects featured by Dezeen from this year’s event, was an exhibition that explores people’s perspectives on forests and a lamp that unfolds like an accordion.

Also on show in the city was the emerging design exhibition Alter, which featured work including an AI-powered tea ceremony and washi paper furniture.

Also this week, automotive brand Fiat launched its Multiplay concept car, which can transform from an SUV into a pickup, with movable seats and an interior designed to be flexible.

Cars were also on the agenda in London, where British car brand Jaguar redesigned its flagship store in Knightsbridge. It is the only place in the world where people can see the recently unveiled Type 01 electric car.

French studio Lacaton & Vassal Architectes, which is led by architects Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal, was named the recipient of the Le Prix Charlotte Perriand 2027.

The studio is known for its social housing designs and was recognised by the Créateurs Design Association & Awards for contributing to contemporary architecture through its work in transforming and improving existing buildings.

Popular projects on Dezeen this week include an arched London apartment building by Alison Brooks, a former workshop converted into a Japanese home and a “quiet yet present” garden studio.

#9054. jean nouvel’s shenzhen opera house takes shape on the waterfront, with completion set for 2028

new construction images reveal the progress of the 220,000 sqm cultural complex, designed around a sweeping roof inspired by the movement of the sea and a program spanning four performance venues.

Designed by Ateliers Jean Nouvel, the Shenzhen Opera House is taking shape along the waterfront of Shekou, in Shenzhen, China, with completion expected by December 2028. Selected through an international competition in 2021 (find designboom’s previous coverage here), the project, titled Light of the Sea, translates its coastal setting into a large cultural complex organized around a fluid roof, expansive public spaces, and four performance venues.

Newly available construction images offer a closer look at the development of the building, moving the project beyond its original competition renderings and into its next architectural phase.

Located in the Dongjiaotou area of Shekou, the opera house overlooks the Shenzhen Bay, with water surrounding three sides of the site. The Paris-based team at Jean Nouvel proposes a sweeping curved roof that evokes the movement of ocean waves. Conceived as a flowing ribbon, the roof gives the complex a continuous profile, establishing a visual connection between the architecture and its maritime surroundings.

The project brings together several performance spaces within a broader cultural destination. Its program includes a 2,100-seat opera hall, an 1,800-seat concert hall, a 1,000-seat small opera hall, and a 500-seat multifunctional theater. These venues are complemented by public facilities, cultural and creative spaces, a stage design and production center, performer accommodation, and offices. Outdoor terraces, a spacious foyer, and public-facing cultural facilities are intended to connect the building with its surroundings.

Acoustic design is particularly important in a building accommodating several different performance formats. The project targets a background noise rating below NR 15, while construction incorporates specialized equipment, including welding and surveying robots, alongside digital design and construction technologies.

Inside the main auditorium, Jean Nouvel’s original design also introduces mother-of-pearl finishes along the curves of the balconies and acoustic wall surfaces. The iridescent material references the shifting reflections of water, extending the project’s maritime concept into the interior architecture.

Construction is expected to continue through the coming years, with the main roof structure scheduled for completion in 2027 and the overall project targeted for delivery in December 2028.

#9053. Yoga and Overweight: Health Benefits and Tips for Getting Started

Part of the beauty of yoga is its accessibility for everyone. Yoga practitioners come in all shapes and sizes and are hella modifiable. If you have overweight, there’s 100% a place for you in the world of downward dogs, crescent lunges, and resting pigeons.

Check out these benefits of yoga for overweight.

For wellness, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more holistic practice than yoga. Your physical and mental health can get a boost from busting out your mat.

The limb-stretching, muscle-engaging, bodyweight-bearing nature of yoga has many physical benefits.

For starters, yoga may enhance your metabolism. An older study found that people who practiced had greater metabolic efficiency and lower weight than non-yogis.

It’s clear, too, that yoga’s combo of cardio and strength torches calories. A 160-pound person can burn around 180 calories per hour, popping in and out of poses. A 2021 study revealed that both Hatha and vinyasa yoga led to weight loss, with an average of 3.4 kilograms (7.5 pounds) lost over a 6-month.

Extra strength and flexibility are two other well-known upsides of the practice. Research shows that even sedentary folks can build these elements of fitness by taking up yoga. One study showed that, after 8 weeks of practicing at least twice a week (180 minutes), people with no prior yoga experience had greater muscle strength, endurance, flexibility, and cardio-respiratory fitness.

On the surface, yoga might look like mere stretching — but the practice goes far beyond the physical. Yoga engages the mind in all sorts of ways that may have benefits for overweight.

By training your brain toward calm and focus, yoga sessions encourage mindfulness. A mindful outlook can have far-reaching effects in multiple areas of life, like promoting mindful eating and greater body awareness.

As a form of self-care, yoga can also promote a healthier body image. In a 2018 study, young adults who made it a habit reported higher satisfaction levels with their bodies. Better self-esteem and motivation have also been linked to the practice.

Then, too, yoga’s stress-relieving effects might follow you off the mat and into the dining room. Some research has found that people who do yoga binge eat less often.

Wanna get started with yoga but aren’t sure how? We got you.

It all starts with setting realistic goals and expectations. If you’ve never practiced before, you won’t be pretzel-ing yourself into challenging poses like scorpion or crow overnight — and that’s OK. Consider setting smaller, step-wise goals, such as attending a 30-minute class twice a week or mastering a few basic poses. Little by little, you’ll work your way up to a more advanced practice.

It’s also wise to select a class (or video) for beginners. Check your gym or yoga studio’s schedule for introductory sessions, and don’t be afraid to let an instructor know before class that you may need some modifications. Most are happy to provide adaptations to make the class a better experience for beginners.

Meanwhile, if you’re pursuing a yoga practice for weight loss, remember to pair it with other healthy lifestyle practices for best results. Though stretching and holding poses burn calories, yoga might not take you to your weight loss goal alone. A balanced diet, cardio exercise, and sufficient sleep are other keys to achieving a healthy weight.

Yoga stereotypes of scantily clad gym babes in impossible contortions might make you feel somewhat intimidated about in-person classes. If you’re concerned that a gym session will make you self-conscious, start with an at-home practice. (YouTube is a treasure trove of classes and instructors explicitly geared for people with overweight.) All by yourself in your living room, there’s no one to impress.

Or, if you’re up for in-person yoga, let your instructor know your needs again. Modifications are always possible.

No matter where you practice, credit yourself for showing up for your health. And, at the beginning of your session, don’t forget to set an intention you find motivating or encouraging, such as “I am caring for my body” or “I am worthy of love and respect.”

Overweight doesn’t have to be a barrier to taking up yoga. Start small, knowing that you’ll get more comfortable with each session. With all the physical and mental health benefits a yoga practice provides — and all the modifications that make it more accessible — it’s worth a try, regardless of weight.

Last medically reviewed on August 31, 2024

#9052. Eight galleries artfully made from concrete

Our latest roundup collects galleries where exposed concrete surfaces form contemplative settings for paintings and artwork.

From high-profile art museums to modest pavilions housing singular artworks, the galleries below illustrate the endless and artful possibilities of concrete.

Among the projects included in the roundup are buildings by Pritzker Prize-winning architects Peter Zumthor, Eduardo Souto de Moura, Tadao Ando and David Chipperfield Architects.

Read on to discover eight concrete art galleries from around the world:

The David Geffen Galleries, USA, by Peter Zumthor

Wrapped in a ribbon of glazing, The David Geffen Galleries is a curving concrete extension to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, designed by Swiss architect Peter Zumthor.

The elevated gallery snakes above street level and spans Wilshire Boulevard. It is supported by seven structural pavilions that are scattered unevenly along its footprint.

Casa das Histórias Paula Rego, Portugal, by Eduardo Souto de Moura

Two pyramid-like chimneys rise from Casa das Histórias Paula Rego in Cascais, Portugal, which was designed by Portuguese architect Eduardo Souto de Moura to house the works of artist Paula Rego.

Enclosed by red-concrete walls, the interior was designed as a sequence of rooms tailored to different formats, from small lithographs to large-scale paintings.

Xiao Feng Art Museum, China, by ZAO/standardarchitecture

Chinese studio ZAO/standardarchitecture created an angular concrete building looping around a central courtyard for the Xiao Feng Art Museum in Hangzhou.

Dedicated to the artist couple Xiao Feng and Song Ren, the gallery rises and falls to form openings that guide visitors under bridge-like elements to the courtyard.

Japanese architect Tadao Ando designed a subterranean concrete dome to house a permanent installation by British sculptor Antony Gormley at Museum SAN in Wonju, South Korea.

Spanning 25 metres in width, the cave-like space was topped by a central oculus that looms over the cast-iron sculptures.

Nubuke Extended, Ghana, by Baerbel Mueller and Juergen Strohmayer

Nubuke Extended is a one-room concrete gallery extension to the Nubuke Foundation in Ghana, which was raised above the ground to form a shaded events and gathering space below.

Designed by architect Baerbel Mueller and architectural designer Juergen Strohmayer, the gallery’s interior features high ceilings and a mezzanine level.

Richard Serra gallery, USA, by Thomas Phifer and Partners

At the Glenstone Museum in Maryland, American architecture studio Thomas Phifer and Partners created a rectangular gallery for the artworks of sculptor Richard Serra.

The building was made from cast-in-place structural concrete with doors made of stainless steel, and a series of skylights provides the only source of light inside.

Anselm Kiefer Pavilion, Germany, by David Chipperfield Architects

Six years after completing the Carmen Würth Forum museum in Germany, architecture firm David Chipperfield Architects returned to the site to add a monolithic concrete gallery built around a singular large-scale artwork.

Once too big to exhibit at the museum, the Schwarze Flocken artwork by Anselm Kiefer now hangs on the wall of the Anselm Kiefer Pavilion, illuminated by rooflights.

Ginkgo Gallery, China, by MORE Architecture

Scooped concrete ceilings animate the Ginkgo Gallery in Jiaxing, which was designed by Dutch studio MORE Architecture as an antidote to China‘s boom of large-scale museums.

Located on an island in a manmade lake, the museum’s board-marked concrete surfaces were arranged to create horizontal patterns across the walls and roofs.

#9051. Starvation Mode: How Caloric Restriction Affects Your Body

Cutting back on calories but not losing weight? You might wonder if you’ve gotten stuck in the twilight zone of so-called “starvation mode.”

Everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight. But is starvation mode really a thing — or just an urban legend?

The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response. To prevent you from losing weight rapidly, your metabolism slows, conserving energy by reducing the calories it burns.

Research shows starvation mode — formally called adaptive thermogenesis or metabolic adaptation — is a legit phenomenon. It’s well documented that sometimes, the more weight you lose (and the more rapidly you do so), the more your body resists the process.

Evolutionarily speaking, this may be a holdover from when humans faced food scarcity and needed a mechanism for self-preservation. But in today’s world, starvation mode can be a frustrating roadblock to weight loss.

What does this metabolic hiccup look like? These symptoms may indicate that starvation mode is becoming a problem for your health:

Starvation mode isn’t the same thing as actual starving. In today’s modern food environment, true starvation is rare. If you’re eating regularly, you won’t experience life-threatening starvation.

However, your body might exhibit some of the same early signs as real starvation. These include the symptoms listed above.

Most commonly, though, starvation mode involves stalled weight loss. You may have hit the wall of adaptive thermogenesis when restricting calories and increasing physical activity without losing weight.

Getting into starvation mode can take just a few days, especially if those days involve severe calorie restriction.

So what counts as severe calorie restriction? Many experts advise not going below 1,200 calories per day for women and 1,500 calories per day for men unless supervised by a doctor. Anything below these numbers could land you in starvation mode faster.

Fortunately, getting your body out of starvation mode isn’t complicated.

First, there’s the obvious solution: Eat a few more calories. But we don’t mean just any calories. By adding a few more nutrient-dense foods (especially those with fiber and protein), you may find weight loss becomes easier, not harder. Both of these nutrients have links to weight loss — so they might help you get out of starvation mode without gaining weight.

If you’re feeling extremely depleted, you might take a temporary break from a weight loss diet to replenish your nutrient stores.

Choosing the proper exercise could also bump you out of starvation mode. Resistance exercises like weightlifting, yoga, push-ups, squats, and others build muscle, which increases your metabolic rate.

According to a 2014 study, people who participated in a 9-month resistance exercise program increased their resting metabolic rate — aka how many calories they burned at rest — by an average of 5%.

Weight loss is a balancing act. It’s normal to experience physical and emotional ups and downs.

That said, it’s time to see a doctor if you’re noticing symptoms like extreme fatigue or lethargy, constipation that lasts more than a few days, sensitivity to cold, or unusual mood changes. Your healthcare team can help you hit the sweet spot of weight loss without lingering in starvation mode.

Despite its name, being in starvation mode doesn’t mean you’ll starve. Instead, it’s a state in which your body has adapted to your weight loss efforts, giving you pushback on how many calories it burns. With strategies like tweaking your calorie intake and adding strength training, you can get out of this mode and back on the path to sustained weight loss.

#9050. Taller Alberto Calleja nestles concrete Casa Nova into tree-filled site on Mexican coast

Photography by Onnis Luque (unless stated otherwise)

A tree-filled “fissure” bridged by elevated timber walkways cuts through the centre of this house on Mexico’s southern coast, designed by local architecture studio Taller Alerto Calleja.

Named Casa Nova, the holiday home is nestled on a long, narrow site overlooking the sea in Mazunte, Oaxaca, and comprises two skinny trapezoidal volumes and a pair of cubic annexes finished in exposed concrete.

Taller Alberto Calleja (TAC) said the design was informed by the site’s narrow sea frontage, which led to the creation of a narrow, tree-filled “fissure” at the site’s centre that frames views to the sea.

“The main strategy was to create a continuous fissure of vegetation and water at the centre of the site, fragmenting the programme into two longitudinal volumes,” the studio told Dezeen.

“The intermediate void becomes the protagonist of the project. Within it, a reflecting pool functions as a gathering and transitional space, connecting both volumes through elevated bridges,” it added.

Casa Nova is divided across the two trapezoidal volumes, with social spaces including the living, dining and kitchen space to the east and a block of bedrooms to the west.

The flat outer edges of these volumes have been left largely blank, while the angled elevations facing the central trees and forest can be opened up entirely via sliding and folding timber screens, leading onto a network of steps, terraces and walkways that link up the site.

These timber screens feature alternating solid sections and angled louvres, allowing light and air to enter the home even when closed.

“The angles, changes in direction, fragmentation and relationship between solid and void create a dynamic architecture whose perception transforms as one moves through it,” said the studio.

“In this context, exposed concrete and wood in its natural state became a logical choice, not only for their inherent qualities and durability, but for their ability to integrate into the surroundings,” it added.

Prow-like terraces on the roof of both volumes extend southwards to capture sea views and overlook a central swimming pool designed to blend with the horizon.

At the back of the site, two cubic volumes contain bedrooms accompanied by their own social spaces, green courtyards and pools, allowing them to be occupied independently from the main home if desired.

Other projects recently completed by TAC include Casa Mavra, a home in Valle de Bravo that contrasts its forested site with two angular volumes finished in black concrete.

Elsewhere in Mexico, Studio Font recently completed Casa Diez Pies, which steps down a lush coastal cliff, and Dosorozco created Casa Sima, a forest dwelling with a textured material palette.

Photography by Onnis Luque (unless stated otherwise)

#9049. sumayya vally’s counterspace to design elie khouri art foundation in dubai

drawing on beirut’s urban fabric and traditional gulf courtyard houses, counterspace will transform an existing jumeirah villa into a new cultural destination with galleries, educational spaces and gardens, opening in late 2028.

Architect Sumayya Vally and her practice Counterspace are appointed to design the permanent home of the Elie Khouri Art Foundation (EKAF), transforming an existing villa in Dubai’s Jumeirah 1 into a contemporary art institution. Expected to open in late 2028, the project will bring together exhibition galleries, educational spaces, pavilions and gardens.  Founded by French-Lebanese collector and philanthropist Elie Khouri, the foundation builds on more than 20 years of collecting contemporary art. Under the direction of Caroline Louca, its program will combine works from Khouri’s collection with changing exhibitions, institutional collaborations, loans and educational initiatives.

For the architectural transformation, Vally draws on the layered urban fabric of Beirut and the inward-facing spatial organization of traditional Gulf courtyard houses. The proposal considers how the existing domestic character of the building can inform a new public identity. Doors, cornices, balustrades and the original arrangement of rooms become starting points for a contemporary architectural language. As Vally explains, the project explores how the intimate geometries of a house can acquire a public scale, with the memory of the existing building informing the future identity of the foundation.

The planned spaces by the Johannesburg-based team at Counterspace extend beyond galleries to include pavilions, a garden, hospitality areas and outdoor settings for seasonal events and gatherings. This mix of exhibition, learning and social spaces reflects the ambition of the foundation to encourage encounters with contemporary art beyond the traditional museum experience. The appointment comes as Dubai continues to expand its contemporary art and cultural infrastructure. While the foundation will draw on a private collection, its program is intended to extend beyond it, creating opportunities for exhibitions, education and exchange with artists and institutions in the UAE and internationally. ‘I hope that artists, designers, researchers and makers from the region will bring other imaginations into the work, and that the institution will continue to acquire forms and meanings we cannot yet anticipate,’ Vally says.

With its opening scheduled for late 2028, the project positions the existing villa as the starting point for a new cultural institution.

Picture this: you're stepping off a direct overnight flight at Dublin Airport, passport in hand, ready to spend two weeks exploring Ireland's Wild Atlantic Way — and the transatlantic crossing that would have cost you $600 per seat cost you just 13,000 Avios instead. That's the moment this redemption delivers. For the ChooseFI community, the math here is almost offensive in how good it is. A round-trip economy ticket from Boston to Dublin on Aer Lingus typically runs $300–$600 per person, and during peak summer travel it can climb even higher. At 13,000 Avios one-way, you're squeezing **2.3 to 4.6 cents per point** out of every Avios you redeem. To put that in perspective, most loyalty program analysts consider 1.5 cents per point a solid redemption. You're potentially tripling that benchmark on what is genuinely one of the easiest award bookings in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. The pricing inefficiency here runs deep. British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart** — meaning the price in Avios is determined by how many miles the plane physically flies, not by what the airline thinks the market will bear on that route. The North Atlantic crossing from the U.S. East Coast to Ireland is, by aviation standards, a relatively short haul. Dublin sits closer to Boston than Los Angeles does. That geographic reality, baked into BA's award chart structure, means you pay a "short-haul" price for what most travelers consider a major international trip. Aer Lingus operates modern Airbus A321LR aircraft on these transatlantic routes — a genuine premium product in economy with dedicated transatlantic seating, meal service, and that unmistakably warm Irish hospitality. This isn't a cramped regional jet. You're flying a purpose-built transatlantic cabin at a fraction of the cash cost. For a family of four, this redemption is transformational. At 13,000 Avios per person each way, a family round trip costs 104,000 Avios total — a points balance that's achievable with a single well-timed credit card welcome bonus. The alternative? Dropping $2,400 or more in cash for the same four seats. That's real money that stays in your FI journey.

The core insight here is understanding what British Airways Avios actually prices — and exploiting the gap between that and what the market charges.

BA's Avios program uses a distance-based award chart. Every flight is assigned a price based on the number of miles between the origin and destination, broken into distance bands. The critical band for this redemption is the one covering flights up to approximately 2,000 miles for partner airlines. Boston (BOS) to Dublin (DUB) clocks in at roughly 3,100 miles — but here's where it gets interesting: Aer Lingus prices these transatlantic short-haul routes within a favorable partner tier that makes the Avios cost dramatically lower than you'd ever pay booking directly.

Layer 1 — You're not booking BA flights. You're using BA Avios to book Aer Lingus flights. This distinction is everything. British Airways-operated long-haul flights carry notoriously high fuel surcharges — often $300–$800 or more on top of the Avios cost, which can completely destroy the value of your redemption. Aer Lingus, as a partner airline, charges no fuel surcharges on Avios bookings. You pay the Avios plus modest government taxes and fees, typically $5–$30. That's it.

Layer 2 — Off-peak pricing drops it further. BA Avios has off-peak pricing for Aer Lingus transatlantic routes, and when you travel in shoulder season, the rate can be even more favorable. The ChooseFI community travels smart: avoiding peak summer crowds and booking shoulder seasons isn't just about lower prices, it's about a better experience overall.

#9047. Text Neck Exercises: Simple Moves to Ease Digital Strain

Whether you’re caught up in doomscrolling or just checking your work emails, chances are you’re spending a lot of time on your phone. But all that screen time can lead to a pesky condition called “text neck.” Hunching over your device can leave you with some severe aches and pains.

So, hold your phone up to eye level and check out these easy tips to get rid of text neck fast!

Also known as “tech neck,” text neck is a term coined by a chiropractor to describe the neck pain you might feel after spending too much time looking down at your phone.

Most of us check our phones with our heads tilted forward and down. When you do this for too long, the muscles in your neck get strained. The muscles in the back are overstretched, while the ones in the front are compressed.

If you have text neck, here’s what you might be dealing with:

But don’t get bent out of shape about overusing your favorite device. There’s no solid proof that your phone habits are to blame for your neck woes. Several studies found no connection between using your device and having neck or shoulder pain.

You could get a sore neck from overusing your muscles for many other reasons, like genetic factors, weight issues, or bad posture. “Text neck” might be a term concocted by a chiropractor to get your business. But, hey, we’re not judging.

To help ease text neck pain, try these simple exercises.

Aside from these cubicle-friendly exercises, here are some ideas to help keep text neck from being a regular pain in the y’know:

“Text neck” is the popular term for the head and neck pain caused by hunching over your device for too long. But don’t throw away your beloved device just yet. More research is needed to link “text neck” to your tech time.

In the meantime, sit up straight and do gentle exercises like neck rolls, chin tucks, and shoulder rolls. To prevent text neck from hitting you up on the reg, take regular breaks from your phone and seek out habits that help lengthen and strengthen your body. Your neck will thank you!

#9046. SABO Project "softens divisions" inside Manhattan apartment

Photography by Alexandre Delaunay

New York and Paris design studio SABO Project has introduced rounded partitions and bold green accents to a compact apartment on Manhattan’s Lower East Side.

The 728-square-foot (68-square-metre) residence was renovated for a family of three with the help of contractor Alexar Interiors.

SABO Project opened up the plan and rounded the corners of walls and partitions between the various functional areas to visually improve the flow.

“The design aims to soften divisions between spaces so the apartment is experienced as a central living room extending into surrounding alcoves,” said the studio.

The apartment carries an industrial aesthetic thanks to exposed breeze-block walls, metal ductwork, concrete ceiling and polished concrete flooring.

Steel structural beams are painted a shade of mid green that is also applied to the lower kitchen cabinets, and appears on curtains and in artwork around the home.

“The apartment balances the rough materiality of exposed masonry blocks and ductwork with the soft textures of bespoke curtains, shades, and rugs,” said SABO Project. “Bold graphic forms animate curtains designed for each room.”

In the open-plan living area, a circular rug in the centre is mirrored on the ceiling by a white-painted circle that’s crossed with a minimalist light fixture.

Along one wall, stacks of concrete blocks with arch-shaped openings form a bench and a display console, accompanied at one end by a small wooden table.

“A long bench runs from the main room into a small outdoor space, conceived as an interior and enclosed with light-filtering fabric and a delicate steel mesh,” said the studio.

This small sun room is accessed via sliding glass doors from the living area and is also visible from the kitchen through a fixed glazed panel.

Here, green outdoor furniture from the Bouroullec brothers’ Palissade collection offers additional seating alongside the breeze-block bench.

Two identically sized bedrooms – one for the parents and another for their child – are decorated with the same colour and material palette as the rest of the apartment.

Quartets of breeze blocks are stacked on their sides to form nightstands with cubbies, and green appears again in the bedding.

In the bathroom, white tiles with green grout get progressively smaller as they reach the ceiling, creating a subtle gradient effect through density.

A lozenge-shaped mirror and sconce, and a basin with filleted corners continue the rounded forms found throughout the residence.

SABO Project was founded by architect Alexandre Delaunay, who works between New York and Paris on a range of residential, commercial and cultural projects.

The studio’s portfolio includes a Brooklyn loft featuring an irregular clustered storage unit, a Parisian apartment with multicoloured flooring and space-saving stairs, and another residence in the French capital that includes peg-hole walls and a curved child-proof staircase.

Photography by Alexandre Delaunay

#9045. Matteo Thun designs Torre Velasca interiors using "building itself as the starting point"

Photography by Alberto Strada (unless stated otherwise)

Italian architect Matteo Thun looked to the original materials and colours of Milan’s iconic Torre Velasca when creating its new interiors, which feature pink hues inspired by the tower’s dusky facade.

Thun has designed 72 flats in the upper floors of the tower, ranging from suites to duplex penthouses. He approached the interior design of the skyscraper, built in the 1950s by the architecture studio BBPR, with a focus on reinterpretation.

“We allowed the masters and the building itself to speak, imagining a way of living within it that would carry the building a little further into the future, adding a new chapter to its history,” Thun told Dezeen.

“We did not seek contrast: our design was informed directly by the materials and colours of Torre Velasca, and we chose not to intervene where we felt the architecture had already achieved a sense of completeness.”

His studio preserved original details, including doors, window frames, loggias and tiles in the bathrooms and kitchens. These were then juxtaposed with modern furniture and evergreen design classics.

“The interiors bring together new furniture designed by the studio and design references spanning the 1950s to the 1980s, including iconic pieces developed in new colourways in collaboration with historic Milanese companies,” Thun said.

“With a deep appreciation for craftsmanship and a strong attention to detail, these designs share an ability to evolve without losing their identity.”

The colour palette, too, was inspired by the original hues of the Torre Velasca.

In the living rooms, walls are covered in custom-made velvet wall coverings by textile company Dedar in a pale pink colour that resembles the pink plaster on Torre Velasca’s facade.

“The building itself was our starting point,” Thun said.

“The pink plaster, developed and patented specifically for the tower, together with the blue and green floor tiles found both inside and in the loggias, formed the basis of our colour palette,” he continued.

“We developed different gradations of these tones, opting for darker shades of green and blue to define the entrance areas and bedrooms. “

As well as the apartments, Thun also designed the interior of the reception, lobby and the corridors on the ground floor.

And while this was an interior project, Thun says it ended up becoming “a lesson in architecture” for his studio.

“Working with a building as distinctive as Torre Velasca challenged us to think and work first and foremost as architects,” Thun said.

“The challenge was not to reinvent the building, but to find ways to make its original character feel relevant today, while remaining true to BBPR’s vision,” he continued.

“In this sense, the project became a process of discovery, with the building itself serving as our greatest teacher. It was, in many ways, a lesson in architecture for us.”

Thun has previously designed the interior of the boutique hotel The Julius Prague and “hotel-like” rooms for a German hospital.

Photography by Alberto Strada (unless stated otherwise)

#9044. pedrali designs a gentle habitat where workplace demands and hospitality make peace at orgatec

returning to orgatec for its ninth time, pedrali stages #pedraligentlehabitat across a fluid sequence of spaces, reflecting the growing overlap between office and hospitality design.

mariana rodrigues November 11, 2026 5 min

Pedrali returns to Orgatec in Cologne for the ninth time, twenty-two years after its debut in 2004, setting up #PedraliGentleHabitat. The Italian manufacturer addresses the reality that rigid desk rows rarely spark great ideas, bringing the comfort of hospitality directly onto the office floor. Answering the fair’s theme, ‘From rooms to relationships: designing spaces in an ever-changing world,’ the setup proves office furniture can be as inviting as it is functional, with interconnected and welcoming environments designed to reflect contemporary lifestyles and evolving professional needs.

Designed by Milan practice DWA Design Studio, the 700 square meter stand takes shape as a warm architectural landscape framed by exposed poplar wood and rippling canvas surfaces that play with light and shadow. Rethinking the temporary nature of trade show architecture, the company designed the entire pavilion to be completely dismantled, packed up, and reused. In fact, major structural components are already enjoying a second life after first appearing at Salone del Mobile 2026.

This circular focus extends straight to the tabletop through Unico, an experimental project developed alongside DWA Design Studio. Instead of discarding the leftover industrial plastic flushed out during color transitions on chair molding lines, the designers press this factory waste into turned plates and bowls that mirror carved stone or primitive clay. The collaboration also scales down the pavilion’s fluid forms with Ondine, a collection of fire-resistant, thermoformed polyester acoustic panels. Taking cues from the stand’s undulating canvas walls, the modular system functions as wall mounts, hanging dividers, or desk screens to keep open-office chatter firmly in check.

Pedrali translates modern work dynamics into focused, tactile environments, starting with an executive meeting setup centered around Robin Rizzini’s architectural Frank table. The structure is paired with Patrick Jouin’s soft, organic Opale chairs featuring solid ash or walnut legs, Sebastian Herkner’s Blume Sideboard, and the Kawara lighting by Yusuke Kawai, whose forms nod to traditional Japanese roof tiles. For active collaboration, Rizzini’s modular Rizz Workstation benches accommodate teams alongside Jorge Pensi Design Studio’s ergonomic Polar task chairs, newly introduced in terracotta and sage green breathable mesh.

Shared social zones do away with fixed seating in favor of fluid interaction, anchored by one of the latest additions unveiled at Orgatec, Busetti Garuti Redaelli’s new Buddy Oasi Serpentine system. The modular setup curves into winding, upholstered islands paired with Patrick Jouin’s cocooning Ila armchairs and the newly introduced castor-mounted Buddy poufs, inviting casual catch-ups. When open-plan chatter inevitably calls for retreat, the new mobile Buddyhub Desks and Sideboards wheel in on castors to carve out instant, acoustic-wrapped focus niches. Workstations transition to the Arki-Table Desk, spotlighting a newly developed integrated lighting system engineered for the collection, while Ondine Desk screens can also be mounted directly onto Arki-Table Desk to ensure acoustic continuity across different workstation families.

The sequence wraps up by dissolving the sharp boundary between indoor offices and the outdoors. Nearby, the Ikon Twist table anchors open-air settings, balanced by Formafantasma’s Estratto coffee tables extruded from single-material aluminum. Weaving acoustic quiet, clean geometry, and raw tactile materials into a single cohesive landscape, Pedrali proves that a well-designed office is not just somewhere you clock in, but an inviting habitat that feels good to spend the day in.

#9043. Bumps Inside Nose: Common Causes and Top Treatments

There are many possible causes for bumps inside your nose — some as harmless as a pimple, others that might need more attention. It’s easy to imagine the worst, but the truth is usually less alarming.

If you’ve got a painful, annoying, or strange bump in your nose, keep reading to learn what it might be, whether it’s worth worrying about, and how to deal with it.

So, what’s behind these bothersome nose bumps? Here are some common culprits:

This is inflammation of the nasal vestibule, the area just inside your nostrils, often caused by bacterial infections. It can lead to painful, red bumps sensitive to the touch. Common triggers include frequent nose-picking, blowing too hard, or even plucking nose hairs.

Like on your face, the pores inside your nose can become clogged with oil, dirt, and bacteria, leading to pimples. These can be painful and may swell, especially in such a sensitive area.

Non-cancerous growths can develop in the nasal passages or sinus lining due to chronic inflammation, allergies, or infections. While they’re usually painless, larger polyps can cause blockages, leading to breathing difficulties, a reduced sense of smell, or recurrent sinus infections.

When you pluck or trim nose hairs, the hair can sometimes grow back into the skin instead of out, causing an ingrown hair. If this becomes infected, it can result in a painful bump inside the nose.

A bump can also form inside the nose due to trauma, such as a blow to the nose, or even from something as simple as aggressive nose-picking. The trauma can cause the tissue to swell or become bruised. In some cases, a hard bump may form as the tissue heals.

Fluid-filled sacs that can form in your nose, usually harmless but sometimes uncomfortable.

A hard bump inside the nose might be due to problems with the cartilage, such as a deviated septum or cartilage overgrowth.

Small, benign bumps that may appear on or in the nose are often mistaken for pimples but are fibrous tissue growths.

Ready to say goodbye to that pesky bump inside your nose? The proper treatment depends on what’s causing it, but here are some ideas to ease the discomfort and promote healing:

Additionally, if you’re dealing with nasal polyps, a healthcare professional might prescribe steroid sprays to shrink them and reduce inflammation, making breathing easier.

On the other hand, if a bacterial infection is the culprit, as in cases of nasal vestibulitis, your doc may recommend a topical antibiotic like mupirocin. This ointment is applied directly inside the nose to target the infection, reduce redness, and promote healing.

While most nose bumps aren’t a big deal, some need more attention. Here’s when to make that appointment:

Even the slightest bump inside your nose can be a major annoyance. Causes vary from harmless pimples to things that require more attention, like polyps.

Self-care measures can usually ease discomfort and speed healing, but if it’s super painful or worrying discharge, it’s time to sniff out professional help.

#9042. Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

By now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy. This class of medications mimics naturally occurring hormones involved in appetite control and blood sugar regulation to treat type 2 diabetes and aid weight-loss efforts. It should be no surprise, then, that conversations around these popular drugs have largely centered on the scale. However, some scientists are starting to look more closely into how they may impact something perhaps even more personal: our sex lives.

At present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll. As the number of people using these medications has soared, so have anecdotal reports about how they’re impacting users’ day-to-day—and yes, this includes things like pleasure and sex drive. Though there hasn’t been a ton of research into the relationship between sexual health and GLP-1s yet, more scientists are starting to investigate potential impacts.

In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry. But how exactly might these drugs impact sex drive? And is there a way to remain engaged in your sex life while on a GLP-1? We tapped experts to find out.

To understand how GLP-1s might influence libido, it helps to walk through how they work more broadly.

Some options, like Wegovy and Ozempic, contain semaglutide, which is a synthetic version of a naturally occurring hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1. Semaglutide binds to GLP-1 receptors throughout the brain and body, helping regulate appetite, blood sugar, and feelings of satiety, James Simon, MD, an ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist and one of the researchers behind the Obesity Pillars study, tells SELF.

Other options, like Zepbound and Mounjaro, contain a different active ingredient called tirzepatide, which mimics both GLP-1 and a related hormone, and thus impacts the body in similar ways to semaglutide.

On top of reporting reduced appetite and increased satiety, a number of patients have also found that these weight-loss medications quiet what they call “food noise.” But as it turns out, the same parts of the brain that control appetite are also responsible for other reward-seeking behaviors, according to Dr. Simon. He says this could help explain why taking GLP-1s may have the auxiliary impact of decreasing appetite for another pleasurable activity: sex.

On top of that, early research suggests that GLP-1s may affect certain serotonin receptors, including one called 5-HT2C. This is thought to be a key player in the sexual side effects often experienced by those taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as reduced libido and delayed orgasm.

“We know that, while SSRIs are fantastic options for anxiety and depression, they can have a significant impact on sexual desire and orgasmic function in both men and women,” says Dr. Simon. “It makes sense that other medications that also impact serotonin pathways might have similar impacts on sexual desire in some individuals.”

Sexual function isn’t just about hormones and brain chemistry. It also depends on the pelvic floor, a group of muscles that support the bladder and bowel, among other organs, and play an active role in arousal and orgasm, explains pelvic-health physical therapist Iris Xu, PT, DPT, of Fusion Wellness & Femina Physical Therapy.

“During arousal the pelvic-floor muscles increase blood flow to the genitals,” Dr. Xu says. During penetration the muscles lengthen and relax to allow for comfortable insertion and boost sensation. And during orgasm they contract rhythmically, creating the pulsing feeling associated with climax, she says.

In general, weight loss—from GLP-1s or other methods—can improve pelvic-floor function because reduced abdominal pressure means the muscles don’t have to work as hard to support the pelvic organs, Dr. Xu says. A 2024 study published in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics found that women carrying more fat, particularly in the pelvic area, had weaker pelvic floor muscles than those with less.

But GLP-1s don’t just encourage fat loss. Because these medications can lead to relatively rapid weight loss, preserving lean muscle mass can be challenging—especially without adequate protein intake or resistance training, says Dr. Xu. “[GLP-1s] can also cause loss of lean body mass and strength, especially when used in isolation without exercise or diet modifications,” she adds. In extreme cases this can lead to a condition called sarcopenia, which some studies have linked to reduced pelvic floor function. (FWIW, muscle loss can occur no matter how you lose weight. But by accelerating the weight-loss process, GLP-1s may speed up muscle loss as well.)

At the time of writing, research specifically examining GLP-1 medications and pelvic-floor outcomes remains limited. There is also little data on these drugs’ impact on muscle loss. But the research we do have points to this being a likely outcome, and Dr. Xu says losing too much lean mass may weaken pelvic floor support. This, in turn, can affect arousal, orgasm intensity, or overall sexual function.

As mentioned earlier, part of the notoriety of these medications is the speed at which many patients lose weight. Research has shown that, on average, people who are overweight or living with obesity can lose anywhere from roughly 10% to 20% of their total body weight on a GLP-1, depending on factors like which drug they use, what dose they take, and how long they continue treatment.

However, despite cultural messages to the contrary, weight loss does not automatically translate to increased body confidence and desire, Joy Berkheimer, PhD, LMFT, a sex and relationship therapist, tells SELF.

“Particularly if you have a long history of having your body policed against external beauty standards—as most women and people assigned female at birth do—the rapidity of the physical changes can lead you to feel unfamiliar in your body,” she says. Sexual desire and pleasure are often closely tied to embodiment, so a lack of embodiment can impact intimacy, she says.

It’s not all bad news; for some people the broader health changes associated with these drugs may actually improve aspects of sexual well-being. People go on GLP-1s for help with a variety of health conditions, such as obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), to name just a few. Addressing these sorts of underlying issues may benefit sexual health.

That means even if the medications dial down some of the brain signals tied to desire, other changes happening in the body (e.g., improved energy, hormone balance, and physical comfort) may help support a healthier sex life, Dr. Simon tells SELF.

“Fat cells are highly inflammatory and impede our well-being far beyond their impact on our weight, leading to things such as joint pain and muscle fatigue,” he says. Feeling weak and achy can reduce interest in any physical activity—sex included!—as well as decrease pleasure during them. But as fat mass decreases and inflammation drops, people may feel more comfortable, energetic, and ultimately sexier. Additionally, as body composition improves, hormone levels may shift in ways that boost sexual desire and function, particularly in those with dysfunction, Dr. Simon says. (Body fat contains enzymes that can convert testosterone into estrogen. When levels of these hormones are unbalanced, it can impact sexual health.)

GLP-1 medications have also been shown to improve markers associated with vascular health, including blood pressure. Healthy blood flow is essential to arousal in people of all genders, says Dr. Simon. For those with vaginas it supports clitoral engorgement, lubrication, and vaginal expansion.

Finally, as metabolic health improves some people will see an increase in their energy levels and feel more comfortable in their bodies, says board-certified bariatric surgeon and obesity medicine specialist Betsy Dovec, MD, FACS, DBOM. For some—particularly those navigating postpartum body changes or the menopause transition—that renewed energy and groundedness can translate into increased confidence and desire, she says.

Taken altogether these physiological shifts can enhance sexual function for some people, even as the medications potentially continue to lower the volume on certain reward pathways.

Of course, our sex lives aren’t driven by biology alone. They are mediated by culture and society, the relationships we’re in, our sense of self and self-confidence, and more. The broader life changes that can accompany weight loss may shift libido north or south.

In a society that often equates thinness with desirability, people who don’t fall into the narrow confines of “thin” may feel undesirable, unsexy, or even undeserving of pleasure. For some individuals changes in body composition toward that supposed ideal may lead to increased confidence.

A 2025 survey from the Kinsey Institute and DatingAdvice.com found that 59% of GLP-1 agonist users said the medication had an impact on their dating life, with a number saying it boosted their confidence. Justin Lehmiller, PhD, a social psychologist, research fellow at the Kinsey Institute, and host of the Sex and Psychology podcast, tells SELF that confidence can have huge impacts on our sexual satisfaction.

“Feeling confident makes it easier to surrender to pleasure and facilitates communicating about our sexual needs and desires, which helps to ensure that we’re getting more of what we want in bed,” he says. “By contrast, when we aren’t feeling confident, it’s easy to get stuck in our heads during intimacy and start worrying about things like how we look.”

For those who are single, increased self-confidence may inspire someone who previously didn’t use dating apps or go out to bars because of body image hang-ups to start putting themselves in situations where connection feels more possible, Dr. Simon says. Meanwhile, in long-term relationships that confidence could translate into greater willingness to initiate sex or say yes to a partner’s advances, he adds. It may also mean someone feels more comfortable experimenting with positions they once shied away from—potentially even discovering ones that bring them more pleasure.

In these cases the reward pathways are still muted. However, because other things that shape sexual desire and enjoyment (like confidence) have increased, patients on these drugs may be experiencing better and/or more sex overall.

“Changes in libido are among the most common concerns people bring into sex therapy,” Dr. Berkheimer says. “But often they are a completely normal response to life transitions or physiological shifts, rather than a sign that something is wrong.”

Desire isn’t static, she explains. Rather, it fluctuates across the lifespan in response to factors like stress, sleep quality, exercise routine, medication, illness, hormones, relationship dynamics, and more. That means any shifts you notice after starting a GLP-1 medication aren’t necessarily a sign that something is off—your body might just need time to adjust, Dr. Berkheimer says. Still, if the change feels distressing or different enough to affect your well-being or relationships, it’s worth bringing up with your doctor.

Sexual health, Dr. Dovec says, isn’t a frivolous concern. “Pleasure matters. Intimacy matters. Feeling sexy matters. These are at the core of quality of life,” she says. Shifts in sexual desire and function can offer useful information about what’s happening in your body more broadly. So if sexual changes happen, talk to your provider. As frustrating or unwelcome as these shifts can be, they’re often temporary or solvable with a provider’s help, according to Dr. Dovec.

Sometimes the solution is as simple as adjusting GLP-1 dosage or timing; other times a clinician may suggest lifestyle changes, like adjusting your diet or exercise routine, or additional treatments that support hormone balance.

Not sure how to start the conversation? Dr. Dovec suggests keeping it simple: “You can just say, ‘Something feels different,’ or ‘I don’t feel like myself sexually.’ You’re not going to shock or embarrass your doctor.”

If you find yourself missing pleasure during this season of libidinal lull, Dr. Berkheimer encourages approaching your body with curiosity rather than pressure and expanding intimacy beyond intercourse. “That can look like slowing down and focusing on sensation instead of performance, exploring non-goal-oriented touch like massage or extended skin-to-skin contact, [or experimenting with] sex toys or pleasure aids,” she tells SELF.

Working with a body-neutral or Health at Every Size (HAES) sex therapist can also help you navigate medication effects, physical changes, identity, cultural conditioning, and more so you can erect an updated pleasure practice that honors the body you’re in now, Dr. Berkheimer adds.

#9041. Five examples of Mesoamerican modern architecture

Mexican architects have been combining principles from ancient architecture with modern techniques. Curator and writer Su Wu picks five examples of this phenomenon from her Mesoamerican Modern book.

Wu’s book, Mesoamerican Modern: Ancient Ideas in Contemporary Mexican Homes, details projects that illustrate this trend, from the 1970s to today, with a focus on residential architecture.

“These homes reflect the complex aesthetic cultures of Mesoamerica,” Wu told Dezeen. She chose the phrase that titles the book over “pre-Columbian” because she wanted to demonstrate that the monumentalism and logic of pre-Columbian Mexican architecture did not end with colonisation.

“I think these homes show instead that rather than being relegated to the past, these Mesoamerican materials, techniques, typologies, and forms are alive in the present and also perhaps inspiration or guides for the future.”

Each shows aspects of monumentalism that recall the stone architecture of the wider Mesoamerican culture, while acknowledging the diversity.

The book tries to depart from projects that just use symbols and focus on the logic of the buildings, noting specific characteristics such as patios as intrinsic the the design.

“For me, the most defining characteristics of Mesoamerican architecture are the ones that reflect underlying principles, rather than the disjunction when symbols become separated from their meaning,” Wu said.

“So throughout the book I wanted to highlight forms that arise from ideas such as the use of light or shadow as a physical object, or how homes are aligned to natural features, or the everyday presence of craft and the handmade, with an expanded sense of beauty as an attenuating consequence.”

Read on for five examples of the Mesoamerican modern style in Mexico with commentary by Wu.

“This 1973 home is one of a few 20th-century homes in Mesoamerican Modern, built by architect Agustín Hernández for his sister Amalia, the founder of Mexico City’s Ballet Folklorico.

“A poet as well as an architect, Hernández is celebrated for injecting ‘Mesoamerican semantics into the brute vocabulary of modernism’, but  wrote most of all about the geometric and cosmic principles at the heart of Mesoamerican architecture, and the ‘mathematical, almost symphonic rhythm’ of Mesoamerican structures and cities.

“His sister Amalia’s home was inspired by the convex forms of seashells as well as by the prominent ocular motifs in Mesoamerican imagery. “

Casa Mobius by Ernesto Gómez Gallardo, 1974

“Built by the architect for his own family in 1974, this house in Mexico City’s San Jeronimo neighborhood is today the studio and home of ceramicist Perla Valtierra.

“Shaped loosely like a mobius strip, with a triangular lattice allowing spaces to fold in upon themselves and a cantilevered living room, the home reconsiders both volumes and typologies, in rooms that are anything but square.

“The house is furnished with an eclectic mix of iconic Japanese, Brasilian and Mexican furniture, including a chair originally designed for the Museo Experimental El Eco in Mexico City by its founder Matthias Goeritz, a close friend and frequent collaborator of Luis Barragan.”

“Architect Teodoro González de León once described the patio as a defining characteristic of a Mesoamerican home, a space that is at once enclosed and exterior, and open to the elements.

“In this house in Estado de Mexico, Mexico City-based architect Fernanda Canales reclaimed land that had been devastated by cattle overgrazing, creating an interlocking series of patios that, in their deliberately undefined sense of function, create more space without having to build more of it.

“Each room in the home, which is approached through a pyramidal foyer with an opening to the sky, looks out onto courtyards or landscape, replete again with plants of the Americas.”

Casa Cometa by Taller Mauricio Rocha + Gabriela Carrillo, 2019

“In this home inspired by the spatial organization of ceremonial Mesoamerican sites, communal areas extend horizontally, while private spaces descend and rise vertically, like a dramatic bedroom tower with a daily view of both the sunrise and the sunset over the Pacific.

“With its overlapping platforms and passageways, the space designed by Gabriela Carrillo and Mauricio Rocha reflects the multiple planes of existence in Mesoamerican cosmology.

“In this house, a walkway weaves under the swimming pool, which itself slips under a long orthogonal platform, cut through with a descending staircase.”

“Casa Monte is a one-bedroom house with no exterior doors. Instead, the house deliberately discourages approach by appearing like a fortress over the tree line, and by its placement on a stepped platform, which creates a sense of separation from the jungle floor below.

“The open space with a pool cutting across the interior suggests the idea that architecture exists foremost as a way to engage with nature.

“Cast by Matos himself in earth-tinted cement on the beach where the house now sits, the home’s hundreds of individual forms were fitted together on-site.”
